Institute of the Incarnate Word

DIRECTORY

OF SPIRITUAL EXERCISES

Curia Generalicia


PART I: THEORY

Chapter 1: What we mean by Spiritual Exercises

1By the Spiritual Exercises “is meant every way of examining one’s conscience, of meditating, of contemplating, of praying vocally and mentally, and of performing other spiritual actions… For as

strolling, walking, and running are bodily exercises, so every way of preparing and disposing

the soul to rid itself of all the disordered tendencies, and, after it is rid, to seek and find the

Divine Will as to the ordering of one’s life for the salvation of the soul, is called a Spiritual

Exercise” [1]. Such was the teaching of St. Ignatius of Loyola, brilliant creator, organizer, and heavenly patron of the Spiritual Exercises.

We also want to imitate the Incarnate Word in his retreat of 40 days in order to conquer ourselves, and order our own lives according to God. 1 For this, we want to know these Exercises in depth and prepare ourselves to preach them fruitfully, disposing ourselves generously without letting an opportunity to preach them pass, according to the occasion2. Already the Spiritual Exercises are one of the preferred apostolates that, in the spiritual dimension, our Institute undertakes3.

2We understand by the Spiritual Exercises its first degree, in its full form of thirty days, and given by one to another4. In actuality, they lend themselves to groups or series. But, in no way, can the possibility of preaching to one alone be excluded, granted that there be subject or capability. We will speak of the other degrees and forms of preaching the Exercises in the sixth chapter.

We believe that the number of suitable directors of the Ignatian Exercises must increase in quantity and quality in order to reach a greater number of all kinds of people each time. But, furthermore, we dream that the day will come when many priests will be capable of “giving” the typical Exercises –one to another for thirty days- so that it may not be “coarse or of little complexion” or only want “to arrive at a certain degree of contentment of soul”, or be “of little aptitude or of little natural capacity”[18], but given to him who “desires to get all the profit he can”[20].

One must return with enthusiasm to this practice, which gave so many fruits of holiness. “They should be given to each one” [18] from which is expected remarkable advantage and fruit for the glory of God or to him who desires to determine the state of life to which God calls him.

If one takes into account that he who “gives to another the way and order to meditate or contemplate, ought to relate the events faithfully …with only a short and summarizing statement” [2]5 and not make conferences, or dictate theology classes, or courses on prayer, or philosophic expositions, or any other spiritual amusement, there would be many who would enliven themselves to carry out this ever-fruitful ministry.

Chapter 2: What the Church teaches

3In fact, the popes have always praised this specific type of Spiritual Exercises. Pope Pius XI affirmed that “the exercises of St. Ignatius are the faultless book of statutes from which all good soldiers of Christ agree to serve” 6, even reproving those who replace them with other less-efficacious methods or those who have tried to empty it of its essential content. “It is a sad reality that the liqueur loses its strength and the machine its power, when it is diluted in the colorless waters of over-adaptation or when some of the fundamental pieces of the Ignatian mechanism are dismantled” 7.

They do not tire of stating their actuality. “As to the asceticism of the Book of Exercises, we could think that Saint Ignatius wrote especially for our epoch” 8; “it is not true that the method has lost efficacy or that it does not correspond to the demands of the modern man”9, but that they are one of the principal means to bring men to a life of prayer and communion with God.

Not in vain did John Paul II proclaim that “for the greater glory of God and the salvation of souls, the goodness of the Creator, in His admirable plan, supplied the Church with a singular help by means of St. Ignatius of Loyola with the limitless promotion of the Spiritual Exercises”10. And in the Post-Synodal Apostolic Exhortation Pastores Dabo Vobis he affirmed that the Spiritual Exercises are “opportunities for spiritual and pastoral growth, in which one can devote more time to pray in peace; opportunities to get back to what it means deep down to be a priest, to find fresh motives for faithfulness and pastoral endeavor”11.

4The CCC established with insistence that seminarians12, priests13, and religious14 annually make the Spiritual Exercises, and also encourages the parochial15 practice of days dedicated to the exercises so that all the faithful may enjoy the benefit that it bestows upon the life of prayer.

Chapter 3: In our Institute

5The Provincial Superiors ought to ensure that all members of our Institute are able to have the Exercises annually, and once every ten years for thirty days16.

6The local superiors must keep a time in mind for the members of their community to have the Spiritual Exercises in their annual calendars.

7Preferably, they are to have the Exercises preached by priests of our Institute, for the greater advantage that they can follow someone who lives the same charism and religious spirit. It is of greater help to the “reform of life” proper to each participant.

8The Provincial Superiors are responsible to coordinate rotations of Spiritual Exercises for the faithful as one of the special forms of our apostolate.

9He, or those in charge, shall look for the most suitable priests for the preaching of the exercises, keeping in mind the suitability of all who are able to give them. The priests seek to be available with generosity.

10The local superiors, those who serve parishes, as well as the other members of our Institute, especially ought to know how to orient those who have “the required fitness” to practice the Exercises.

11Given the importance of the preaching of the Spiritual Exercises, it is necessary that the priest-members of our Institute prepare themselves diligently for this ministry. This begins in the stages of formation in the seminary with the theoretic study of the Spiritual Exercises in the corresponding courses. A practical introduction as assistants or collaborators in rotations is likewise recommendable for the seminarians.

12At times it helps to have the collaboration of various priests in the actual preaching, but there should always be one sole director of the exercises to whom the others correspond to give structural meditations from themselves.

Chapter 4: Essential Characteristics

13Pius XII taught: “The Exercises of St. Ignatius will always be one of the most efficacious means to achieve the spiritual regeneration of the world and its return to right order, on the condition, however, that the Exercises remain genuinely Ignatian” 17. Now then, the “elements that tradition holds as essential in order that the Spiritual Exercises conform themselves to the Ignatian method” 18 are: the end, the means, the manner, and the adaptation.

Article 1: The end

14The end of the Ignatian Exercises is double, as two sides of the same coin: a) “to conquer oneself” and b) “to regulate one’s life without determining oneself through any tendency that is disordered” [21]. They are two essential ends of which, ontologically considered, the primary is “to regulate one’s life” and secondary “to conquer oneself”; and chronologically considered, the primary is “to conquer oneself” and the secondary “to regulate one’s life.” These ends are none other than the gospels: deny yourself (Matthew 16:24) and repent (Matthew 3:2; 4:17; Mark 1:15; Acts 2:38; 3:19).

Article 2: The means

15The means to reach this end are:

a- Acceptance of the ideal (Principle and Foundation)

b- Purification of the soul by compunction (First week).

c- Total offering to Christ (The temporal King).

d- Knowledge and love of Christ (Second week).

e- Ordering of the three potencies:

-Intelligence (Two standards)

-Will (Three classes of men)

-Heart (Three kinds of humility).

f- Election and/or reform of life.

g- Knowledge and love of Christ (Third and fourth weeks).

h- Life of union with God (Contemplation to gain love).

i- To enable the participant with knowledge of how to proceed forward (Ways of prayer, examinations, rules for the discernment of spirits, directions for eating, for almsgiving, to understand scruples, to feel with the Church).

Article 3: The manners

16The ways or manners of using these means, which constitute the Ignatian method, in order to reach the end, are the following:

a. Perfect recollection;

b. To draw grace by means of colloquies, supplications, penitence;

c. Vital activity in the meditations;

d. Permanent reflection upon oneself, above all by means of:

- Particular examination and especially the examination of the meditation

- Continual attention to interior movements;

e. Exposition of documents in the midday talks.

Article 4: The adaptation

17One of the essential elements of the Ignatian Exercises is the adaptation, rightly understood.

a. We want to note that it is essential to an authentic and profound sense of fidelity to the Ignatian text, to adapt the Exercises, as distinct variables intervene: the participant, the enemy, grace, and the director. Leaving the end intact, one must adapt the Exercises in just measure, neither more nor less. The adaptation makes it possible that they reach this end using these concrete means and with these determined ways, also adapted.

18b. In addition to that, it is necessary to modify the “additions” [73-90] of each week (for the second week [130-131], for the third week [205, 206 y 209], and for the fourth week [229]), and must keep in mind that St. Ignatius himself foresaw the necessary adaptations. For example: “It is necessary sometimes to shorten the week, and at other times to lengthen it” [4], and again, “the Spiritual Exercises have to be adapted to the dispositions of the persons who wish to receive them, that is, to their age, education, or ability” [18]; with the goal of reaching the proper end of the first week, more meditations can be given- according to the Vulgate [71]; the number of exercises per day “as age, condition of health, and the physical constitution of the exercitant permit” can be five or less [72]; “it is often useful to make some change” [89]; if one has remained weak, it is better that sometimes they do not rise at midnight [129]; at times it convenient even when one is “strong and well-disposed” [133]; “according to his progress, may lengthen or shorten this week. If he wishes to lengthen it…to shorten it…” [162]; “if one wishes to spend more time…if he should wish to spend less time…” [209]; “the shortening or lengthening of the mysteries,” [226] etc…

19Like all pastoral undertakings, the Spiritual Exercises are also part of what St. Gregory the Great called “the art of all arts”19, and in the arts, shades, accents and proportions have their importance. In this regard, for those who give many Exercises and have many repeat participants it can be useful to give some color to the Exercises, to the points given. For this, basing them in a good index of materials, by means of brief phrases, can give distinct impression to the Exercises. For example: Eucharistic (texts of St. John Eudes), missionary (Redemptoris Missio of Bl. John Paul II), Marian (St. Luis Marie Grignion de Montfort), liturgical, biblical (a good concordance), of spirituality (St. Catherine of Sienna, St. Teresa of Jesus, St. John of the Cross, Bl. Elizabeth of the Trinity, St. Teresa of the Andes, St. Edith Stein, St. Luis Orione, St. Pio of Pietrelcina, etc.), poetic (with anthology of religious poetry), patristic, etc.

Chapter 5: The most important: Prayer

20The most important part of the Spiritual Exercises are the “exercises” [45], called at times “meditation” [45] or “contemplation” [101]. The principal art of the director is to teach the one on the exercises to pray.

Article 1: Distinct forms of prayer

21It can be helpful to explain the distinct methods of prayer that the book of the exercises brings to the participant.

a. Meditation is to consider the great truths of the faith with the powers of the soul. The memory ought to remember, the intelligence to discourse, and the will to love. It is a reasoned discourse of the intelligence about a revealed truth in order to convince us more of its truth, to love it more, and to put it more into practice.

22b. Contemplation is an intuitive gaze of the intelligence in order to penetrate more profoundly into the works of Our Lord, so that the participant moves oneself more to love and imitate him more in their behavior.

23c. Repetition is when one meditates (or contemplates) for a second time and with greater attention on a subject already exercised, returning to consider the same point in order to draw some profit or amplify some aspect of the subject given, paying greater attention to the parts in which he had experienced greater movements (of consolation or desolation) [62] [118,119].

24d. Summary is when “that the intellect, without any digression, diligently thinks over and recalls the matter contemplated in the previous exercises” [64]. The summary tends to leave the ideas well-fixed in the mind.

25e. Application of the senses, “to apply the senses” [133] to the contemplated subject, is “the aid of the imagination to apply the five senses to the subject matter” of the contemplations already made [121]. Our senses should attempt to perceive what occurs there. “The fifth exercise, that is the application of the senses, is very easy and useful, imagining that we see the persons, and hear the words or the noise if there is any; and touch or kiss the places or the persons, a thing which we ought to do with great reverence, modesty, and fear. The sense of smell serves to smell the fragrance of the gifts of God, and the taste, to savor the sweetness; each one of which asks a certain presence of the object or the persons of whom we meditate, accompanied by taste and tender love toward them” 20.

The director should attain that the participants acquaint themselves and experiment all these forms of prayer.

Article 2: Three methods of prayer

26f. St. Ignatius also indicates three methods of prayer, which we ought to know, experience, and teach [4, 18].

1º The first concerning the Ten Commandments, or the capital sins, or the potencies of the soul, allowing the soul to rest on each of these; and consider them for a brief time, trying to draw the greatest fruit possible from each point [238-248].

272º The second is to reflect upon each Word of the principal Christian prayers (Our Father, Hail Mary, etc.), without rushing from one word to the next but allowing the praying soul to remain as long as seems necessary in the consideration of each word [249-257].

283º The third is rhythmic; it attempts to achieve that in each breath one says a word of the principal Christian prayers, (Our Father, Hail Mary, etc.) and in this brief instant consider the most advantageous point that the soul can take from it; be it the meaning of such a word, the lowliness of oneself, etc. [258-260].

Article 3: The principal parts of prayer

29The principal parts of prayer are four: the preambles, the body, the colloquy (or the colloquies) and the examination.

a. The preambles

30There are five preambles:

1º. To put yourself in the presence of God “the intellect raised on high, considering how God our Lord is looking at me” [74], [75], [130] and [239].

2º. To ask to do all Ad maiorem Dei gloriam has a capital importance for the achievement of the end of the meditation, and is to ask God Our Lord that all my intentions, actions and operations may be directed purely to the service and praise of His Divine Majesty [46]. This prayer should always be at the beginning of all meditations or contemplations [49].

3º. To bring to consideration the history and the events that we ought to contemplate [102].

4º. To make the composition of place bringing into memory the circumstances that compose the story, to see the place, the movements, the gestures, etc., “see with the sight of the imagination the corporeal place where the thing is found which I want to contemplate” [47], [103] and [105].

5º To ask God that he grant us to obtain the fruits and graces proper to the meditation that is to be done. This is the petition and the end of each exercise.

b. The body

31The body of the prayer in the exercises is the meditation or contemplation properly said; it attempts to apply the potencies of the soul to the assigned subject. The intelligence reasoning, the will moving, and the memory remembering disposes the soul more to reach the end of the meditation or contemplation. There are not two souls that pray in the same manner. Each soul ought to make use of these resources in such a way that they better help him to consider the subject proposed, and to draw from it the greatest fruit possible [50][51][52].

c. The colloquy or colloquies

32The colloquy (or the colloquies) is to speak with Our Lord as one friend speaks to another, or as a servant to his master, either asking some grace, blaming oneself for some misdeed, or simply telling and asking advice from our Lord [54].

d. The examination

33In the examination, which is to last approximately 15 minutes in Exercises of one month, one ought to analyze how one has made the meditation or contemplation, with the firm resolution to improve in the next exercise [77].

Article 4: The examination of conscience

34g. Another form of prayer, and one which always should be considered as such, is the examination of conscience. St. Ignatius recommends two ways of making this examination:

- The particular exam involves two times of the day, at noon and at night. The soul examines itself regarding a particular defect, which hinders him the most, which disturbs him more and that he considers as the root of many others, or in the better practice of a determined virtue in such a manner that he makes a firm resolution to amend himself of these errors for the following hours. This exam is of great profit for all souls that efficaciously desire to advance in the spiritual life. In order to win the war against Satan, we ought to first defeat him in each battle, which means to conquer our principal defects [24-31].

35- The general examination consists in, for a brief space of time, examining oneself regarding what has occurred in the day, of the sins of thought, word, deed, and omission. It has five steps:

- To give thanks to God our Lord for favors received during the day.

- To ask for grace to know my sins and to rid myself of them.

- To demand an account of my soul up to the present examination.

- To ask God pardon for all our faults.

- To resolve to amend with the grace of God [43].

Article 5: The election

36h. Another form of prayer speaks in direct relation to the essential element of the Spiritual Exercises of St. Ignatius: to regulate one’s life [21]. It refers to what St. Ignatius calls “the election” [169 ff.], or choosing the will of God in each determined situation.

Article 6: An ordered spirit

37All good choices ought to consist of a necessary presupposition: that “as far as depends on us, our intention must be simple. I must consider only the end for which I am created…Hence, whatever I choose must help me to this end for which I am created…therefore, my first aim should be to seek to serve God, which is the end and only after that, if it is more profitable, to have a benefice…for these are means to the end [169]. It is the fundamental element, to want what God wants, whether it is convenient or not for the personal interests of each one [making the Exercises]. It is this spirit that must mark a holy election. If this desire is not well ordered, it will be very easy to error and stray in the result.

Article 7: Matter of the election

38The matter that one submits to judgment ought to be indifferent or good in itself, that is to say, one must aim to choose what is seen to be for the greater glory of God and the salvation of souls; one must always choose between what is good and what is best. Evidently what is contrary to the norms of the Holy Catholic Church cannot enter into the subject of an election (and likewise, one would not be able to pose as the subject of an election the work of following the commandments or not, regarding this there is no need to deliberate because the will of God is clear) [170-171]

Article 8: Times

39There are three times for making a good and healthy election [175-188]:

a) The first time is a special grace of God, in which the soul, without hesitation or the possibility of hesitation follows what is shown to it. God manifests himself in such a way to the soul that it has the joy of full security in knowing that this is the will of God, and it does not occur to the soul to think of the fact that God could will the contrary [175].

40b) The second time is when the soul considers the experiences of consolation and desolation and applying to these the rules of discernment of spirits [313-327 and 328-336], it understands the clear and precise manifestation of God’s will. This requires that the soul thoroughly examines the motions that move it so that it can determine with certainty and security the will of God. [176].

41c) The third time is, having as objective the end of man, that is, that “man is born… for the praise of God our Lord and for the salvation of his soul”, one chooses the most fitting help to the said end [177].

It is necessary to note that one must apply the latter in time of tranquility, that is to say, when the soul is not agitated by diverse spirits and can use its powers without being influenced, that it can act with full liberty and with a clear mind. If one does not keep this point in mind, it is probable that the result of the election may be unsuccessful. If there is no time of tranquility it is suitable to wait until it arrives. The third time has two ways:

42The first way consists in the following steps:

1º Place before my mind the proposed subject, about which I desire to make an election [178]

2º Reconsider the end, that “I am created for the praise of God our Lord and the salvation of my soul” [179].

3º Ask God for the grace that He moves my will and my soul to choose that which better serves His glory and praise, in such a way that my intelligence and my will are guided in accord with His holy will [180].

4º To consider “rationally” all the benefits and advantages that follow from the choice of one of the two extremes of the election; such an office, state, etc. Likewise, to consider all the ills and dangers that will accrue to me in making this choice of office, state, etc. On the other hand, the same is to be done with the opposed proposition, that is, to look at all the benefits and advantages in not taking the said office and all the ills and dangers that follow from this. It is to say, to see all the pros and cons in each case. When they are important decisions, it would be advisable that they think of them thoroughly, and that they encounter all the reasons that there are in one case or the other, and that they are written with clarity and breadth [181].

5º. The most important point is that one tries to make a rational judgment, meaning that examining it in writing or in thought, one judges which reasons have more weight and from where follows the greatest good for my soul, always having in mind the end for which God has created us. Rational judgment and not sentimental; here the sensible appraisal of what I would like, what is more comfortable or easier, must be left aside. It is reason which must dominate in an election. [182].

6º. Having made the election, we must offer it before God, “that the Divine Majesty may deign to accept and confirm it if it is for His greater service and praise” [183].

43The second way [184-188] contains the same steps as the previous, differing only in number four. St. Ignatius wants us to gain objectivity; that we are not moved by our own interests but by those of God, and he presents us four rules, one proposition, and three situations to consider thoroughly.

1st rule: To consider what is that I am going to choose and see the relation that this has with God, my final end, “so that before one chooses he should perceive that the greater or less attachment for the object of his choice is solely because of His Creator and Lord.” [184]

2nd rule: To represent to myself a man whom I have never seen or known, and desiring his full perfection, to think of what I would say to him regarding the matter proposed for the election, searching for the greater glory of God and the salvation of his soul, and to apply to myself such advice [185].

3rd rule: To place myself in articulo mortis, that is to say, in the moment in which I am to leave this world and present myself before God, imagining this situation, to consider what my thoughts would be in respect to the election, in this moment, what I would have wished to do. By this determination I shall guide myself now [186].

4th rule: To place my soul before the judgment of God, the most decisive moment of life, before the Supreme Judge and all the celestial court, and consider what I would then wish to have chosen in order to show this before God, and the rule that I would then have wanted to take, I will take it now, because then I will find complete happiness and joy [187].

44It is necessary that we all learn and familiarize ourselves with these admirable rules of election, and that we know how to apply them in all the situations of our life, so that we are always guided (even in the smallest and most childish decisions) by the wise divine affection, since “the will of God is always, invariably, adorable” 21.

Chapter 6: Degrees of the Spiritual Exercises according to the fruits that follow from them

45In this chapter we speak of the classification and division of the degrees and forms of the Spiritual Exercises of St. Ignatius according to the fruits which they naturally ought to produce in persons well disposed. This will greatly help the preachers, we think, by two ways: first, because it makes him see the great array of possibilities and distinct applications that the Ignatian Exercises have in all their fullness, giving a great liberty to the time of choosing the form that is most convenient to the concrete circumstances, without getting stuck in one determined form, but without losing sight of the end. Second, it will help during the preaching itself, since its end, what the Exercises seek to give or preach, has already been made crystal clear, and it will permit the director to know with precision:

a) what it is that one must search for, in its totality and in each moment, that which will serve it as governing criteria of the infinite applications to preach the Exercises and it will be the guide of all his actions, presenting with clarity also to the exercitants what it is that they ought to obain;

b) what it is that one must hope for willingly from the well disposed exercitants, in what moment and in what way; all of which will be determinant to the time of direction of souls during the Exercises;

c) what it is that can be claimed, that is to say, what are the limits of each degree of Exercises and of each type of exercitant, in such a way that one cannot exact from anyone things that are beyond what they are able to give, and one cannot impose on anyone “things that he could not easily bear” [18].

46Speaking of the Spiritual Exercises of St. Ignatius, in all their forms and degrees, we ought to understand that that which they constitute insofar as it is the specific intention of “conquest of self and regulation of one’s life in such a way that no decision is made under the influence of any inordinate attachment” [21], as is already figured on the cover of the book of the Exercises itself. This constitutes a concrete spiritual effect, which is complex in its totality of partial effects that ought to gradually and successively reach this22. According as one is brought more or less closer to this end considered in its totality, we can classify then the degrees of Spiritual Exercises. The highest degree is constituted by the complete Exercises called such because it respects the thematic outline of St. Ignatius in all its fundamental elements, whether it be given for a month or in its repetitions of a week, and because it searches for the end of the Exercises it its totality. This will be discussed in article 1. The following degrees, of which we will speak in the following articles, and characterized by the reduction of the Ignatian outline (that is taken partially) or in some cases by the function of the exercitant (less discursive and more passive), differ substantially from the first degree because they search partially for the fruits of the Ignatian Exercises.

Article 1: The complete Exercises

47In those called “complete Exercises” the director “gives” the matter, form, and mode, asking moreover for an account of all the motions that pass through the soul. The principal work is done by the exercitant, and consists in the discursive considerations. The director does little as a speaker and much as a spiritual director. Some of the rest of the degrees of Exercises which we shall see later have a greater relevance to the preaching of the director; the exercitants having a more passive role.

48This first and principal “degree” of the exercises can, nonetheless, be subdivided into distinct concrete applications:

a) The complete Exercises in their forma plena are those which are given in 30 days, with the election of state.

b) Another form is when they are for 30 days without an election of state.

c) Also they can be completed, but with a determined time each day dedicated to the Exercises (Cf. [19]), or they can also be divided into two parts of 15 days each.

d) In this category enters the more brief repetitions of the complete Exercises23:

i. The annual repetitions, of 8 to 10 days.

ii. The repetitions made previous to the profession of vows or the reception of Holy Orders.

Fruits

49When the entire Exercises are given and done this complete spiritual effect is sought in its totality, characteristic of the Exercises of St. Ignatius. In the other degrees of Exercises, which we will see in the following articles, only partially does it search for this effect, according to the capacity and disposition of the exercitants, and the circumstances, and way of preaching themselves.

If in this first degree we are able to establish a subdivision according to its concrete mode, a similar classification follows also for the awaited fruit, in proportion to the realization of each of the indicated concretizations from the total fruit of the exercises. For this reason the analogous principle, where one awaits the totality of the fruits, is the typical case of the exercitant capable of making the month-long Exercises, for the first time, in the same order of which St. Ignatius thought, and that one is subjectively found in the best of dispositions [20], wanting to take advantage of them in the greatest degree possible (what we have called the forma plena).

50Extrinsic end: P. Calveras indicated that the extrinsic end that St. Ignatius evidently proposed (finis operantis) to give to these Exercises was the stirring up of vocations to the apostolic life. That is why he chose apt subjects from those whom he hoped with good reason that God would call if they were adequately disposed24.

51Intrinsic end: The intrinsic and proximate end25, complete and composed of the Exercises is a firm and permanent disposition of the soul to be able to love and serve in all things the Divine Majesty. This is the principal and consummate fruit of the Exercises26, that naturally derives from three concrete fruits: to conquer oneself, to regulate one’s life, and spiritual formation that one is given in the Exercises, particularly by means of the experience of discernment of spirits and of the movements27.

52The remote intrinsic end is the perfection of the Christian life, which in its highest degree is holiness. The complete well done Exercises produce the substantial perfection of the Christian life28, because in fact it orders the will so much in its propositions, decisions, and actions from its free and elective part, that in the impulsive and affective dispositions of the heart, which it has placed in God alone, correcting furthermore the false formed concepts and practical judgments. The integral perfection of the Christian life is the work that one ought to make during the rest of one’s life, bringing to perfection the full drawing of which only the first lines were sketched during the Exercises29.

53To conquer oneself

It means to conquest the dominion of the interior kingdom, where “all of our lower faculties [are brought] into greater subjection to the higher” [87], as St. Ignatius said. This is the subjection of reason to God, the dominion of the sensuality, and the full subjection of the inferior parts. In order to subject the rational part to God it is necessary to attain the conquest of the will, that assumes not only a decided and efficacious will, but also to dominate over the impulsive tendencies and the fundamental affective dispositions. This dominion of the rational part additionally carries with it a parallel work in the understanding, in order to reform the formed concepts and practical judgments, to the end that the value of persons and things and norms of conduct refer completely to the esteem and will of God30.

In the conquest of the will, or the perfect order of love, P. Calveras indicates the steps that the well-disposed exercitant proposes31, and that assumes a parallel work regarding the intellect to reform the formed concepts32. The exercitant thus proposes to himself:

1º. Hatred of his sins, grave and minor; hatred of that which without bringing about sin is disordered in his works; and hatred of the world and its spirit [63]; to the end that these hatreds replace whatever attachment or disordered love there is in the soul. By this, in the light of faith, the soul presents to itself the maliciousness of sin and disordered works, the irrationality and disorder of the world and its origins.

2º. The ridding of all actual affection or aversion that self-love has risen in its valor before the real or imaginary presence of sacrifice or the cross [157]. This implies correcting natural judgments that looks at the privations, humiliation and suffering (components of the cross) as opposed to its proper excellence and happiness, through the intimate penetration of the great profit that for its proper perfection, peace, and interior joy of soul and for the divine glory, the cross carries, when accepted in desire and in reality.

3º. The ordering of all particular loves of persons or indifferent things to the reference of God alone [16, 50, 153-155, 184, 338, 342].

4º. Intimately falling in love with the person of Jesus Christ, which brings one to feel His sufferings and glory as his own [203, 221]. He asks for the “intimate knowledge of our Lord” [104] which St. Ignatius mentions, and with it the reference of these mysteries to himself: “who has become man for me” [53, 104].

5º. The perfect order of natural love of oneself, to the extent of searching the promotion of one’s own excellence and satisfaction of the desire of happiness in God and only through God [234-237]. This is incompatible with natural judgment that errantly believes that excellence and happiness consist in worldly greatness and the love of creatures.

6º. Moved in God, highest good and highest perfection, from all weight of love and complacency [237], to know internally the infinite perfections of God [237].

In order to obtain all this, the sole path is the internal action of the exercitant, that with his work he disposes himself to the divine action in the soul33. “For it is not much knowledge that fills and satisfies the soul, but the intimate understanding and relish of the truth” [2].

From the first moment, the Principle and Foundation, St. Ignatius accompanies these objectives with the reform of the practical judgment by the rule of “in as much as” [23]: first, he establishes that which is not founded in the reason of pure divine service is disordered and avoidable; and second, he places as first practical principle, valid always and in all things without exception nor possible dispensation, to do in every case that which better leads us to our final end, what is most pleasing to His will[151, 180].

The dominion and subjection of our sensibility to the rationality is a lifelong task, in a fight where our enemies are the rebellion of our flesh, the natural inclination to what is easiest, and the innate esteem of our natural cogitative that considers what is easy as pleasing and good34. Nonetheless, a month of intense exercise cannot lessen the beneficial and efficacious influence of dominion of oneself. If one cannot obtain well the correction of disorder due to external factors, it is still possible to order the internal factors definitively. These achievements must be accompanied and increased for the rest of one’s life35.

54To regulate one’s life

It is to put order in all acts of the person, in all that relates in some way with oneself and depends, directly or indirectly, on the will36, as far as it is susceptible to order. This assumes a concrete analysis of our actions in the light of faith in order to discover what points are in disagreement with the ideal of perfection proportionate to our state. The first moment of the regulation of life is negative, since one must rid oneself of all evil and imperfection, beginning with the most grave, in order to pass to the second moment, which is to conform the life, by means of concrete decisions, with the ideal Jesus Christ presents to us.

In subjects in which there is a general norm (the commandments, precepts of the Church, the rule for religious, etc.) to order means simply to mold our actions to them. Not all, that in this part falls under need of amendment and perfection, will be completed within the month of the Exercises, but the Exercises will give the subjects in need of amendment and reform for all one’s life. Exercitants must in fact amend themselves from mortal sin and those venial sins which are fully deliberate, at the determined time that one sets their will to continue fighting against their minor faults, including the fight against imperfect habits and defects of character37.

In subjects that do not have a general norm, one searches the will of God in every case, and orders their acts according to this. In this respect, in the first place enters the state or manner of life and the principal occupations that indicate the general orientation of the activities of the person. Within the proper state and office there must be order in the use and distribution of the goods of fortune, and many other particular things that are able to serve diversely for the greater glory of God and the greatest good of the soul. Within these goods, the distribution and order of time itself, and the distribution of activities, etc. hold an important place. Everything that touches upon the reform of life ought to be subject to the rules of election in order to see effectively if this is the reform that God wants. To enter into the matter of elections, diverse from the amendment of habits (which one can find within the first moment of the Exercises), one must wait for the moment in which the soul finds itself properly ready, having removed all the disordered affections (Cfr. [1])38.

55The spiritual formation: discernment

The Spiritual Exercises are a strong experience of intense spiritual life in themselves. From there the efficaciousness of all things comes, especially producing the two indicated fruits. This experience of spiritual life, robust and profound, can be expressed synthetically in the following points39:

1. The continued dealing with God, during the greater part of the day, with the diverse forms of spiritually “exercising oneself”, and in a fitting context.

2. The prayer of supplication that pervades colloquies and the different forms of prayer, and presents to God the graces of which we are in need.

3. Moral instruction and refinement of conscience.

4. The constant reflection upon oneself, by means of the examinations, in their diverse moments and modes.

5. The experience of consolations and desolations and of the rousing of various spirits.

6. Practical exercise of searching for and discovering the will of God in particular things.

7. The use of penances and mortifications, spiritual reading, and the reception of the sacraments.

8. Initiation in the practice of the divine presence.

The book of the Exercises contains methods, instructions, and rules of how to proceed with perfection in each one of these parts of the spiritual labor, and it proposes to the exercitant the practical exercise of all this during an entire month. It establishes the bases and teaches discernment in order to bring forward a serious spiritual life that combines the elements of asceticism and mysticism in theory and practice40. Likewise in the complete Exercises and their repetitions as well as in the inferior degrees, the talks given by the director, generally before noon, are fundamental for spiritual formation of one’s whole life.

Fruit of the repetitions

56As we have said, the complete Exercises can have shorter repetitions, which may be periodic (annual) or previous to some special occasion, like the reception of Holy Orders, or the profession of vows, or before some mission or special apostolate that one must confront.

In the annual repetitions, the end which is sought depends on the dispositions of the exercitant, because if he has lost, in some or in many points, the acquisition of the spiritual dispositions from the month of the Exercises, it is clear that the first intention of the repetition is to redo the point in which he has grown lax. If he has persevered in the fruits of the month-long Exercises, the repetition should have as its object to renew and reaffirm the fundamental dispositions and go forward positively in the knowledge of God and of oneself, and the ordering the new situations or realities which have arisen to Him.

In the Exercises given previously to a special occasion, to these ends proper to the repetition are added the preparation of the soul for the upcoming concrete event. This implies that one’s general dispositions are concretized into particular dispositions necessary in order to fruitfully receive Holy Orders, or take vows, or undertake a specific apostolic work, or depart for a new mission, etc.

Persons

57As we have previously indicated, and as St. Ignatius himself expresses, the complete Exercises in their full form are destined for those “that have subject”, or the capacity and dispositions necessary to complete them fruitfully, without losing time nor to make it a waste for the one who gives them. For those who do not “have subject”, or for those who for different reasons we are not able to expect the complete fruit from them, there are other degrees of Exercises that we will later develop. The efficacy of the Exercises to bring about a life of holiness, the indications of the Magisterium about its value41, the insistence of the saint himself when he proposed making them42, and the experience of centuries further promotes the realization of the Exercises by all who are in the right conditions and arrange the necessary time.

Subjects

58We will not speak here of the subject of the complete Exercises in their full form. This is found written and developed in The Book of the Exercises of St. Ignatius, on which there is an abundant bibliography43. We will only make some specifications. Within this scheme that St. Ignatius thought of and desired for the Exercises, he indicates that the subject matter must adapt itself to the dispositions of the exercitant [4]. Hence, among other reasons, it is suitable that one manifests to the director the state of his soul and the diverse motions that pass within it [6, 17]. If this principle of adaption is valid in the 30-day Exercises, it is also reasonabe to apply this to the repetitions and the shorter forms. Since, as we have indicated, the fruits which are hoped for depend on the dispositions or circumstances of the exercitant, the subject matter ought to order the exercitant according to these concrete fruits.

Father Calveras teaches that in the annual repetitions one ought to insist on the points most necessary to the soul of the exercitant, insisting on those ordered to recreate the dispositions that may have been lost44. For the remaining cases, he gives as a general rule to condense proportionately the four weeks to the days of repetition, insisting more there where the divine grace communicates itself more, and even taking other materials that, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, are of good use to the sought end45. Applying the indications of the Directory for the members of the Society of Jesus, Father Calveras explains that the meaning of the arrangement of following the scheme of the complete Exercises in proportion and method ought to be fulfilled more exactly the first two or three times, in such a way that one masters the Exercises and knows to give them profitably. Afterward, one can proceed with more ease, particularly applying the meditations to the religious state and to their proper vocation, with greater insistence during the exercises of the second week46. It can be, so to speak, “of benefit to the vocation, to the three vows, to the reasons to renew these, to the same formula of our vows, to the divine benefits, to the danger of tepidity and to other like circumstances; …and in general the subjects are such that are valued to increase the fear and love of God, the hatred of oneself, the love of virtue, the contempt of visible things, the desire of the eternal and the ardor of charity” 47. The Exercises are of the same value “in special circumstances” (before Ordination, vows, missions, etc.), adapting the subject to these.

Time

59The complete Exercises in their full form will finish in thirty days, more or less. We believe that the annual repetitions ought to be at least five days and when possible eight.

Distinction between the first degree of Exercises and the other degrees

60According to St. Ignatius, there are three fundamental degrees by which one can divide the Exercises: the complete Exercises, of which we have already spoken, the Exercises of the first week, and the light Exercises48. The first degree distinguishes itself from all the rest primarily by virtue of the fruit which it will seek, the complete and complex fruit, not reduced; and consequently by reason of the subject matter. Furthermore, we will add a category that brings one nearer in some way to the last two degrees indicated: this deals with the preached Exercises, within which is included the retreats in general.

Article 2: Exercises of the first week

61It is when one seeks fundamentally the fruit of the first week (partial with respect to the complete fruit of the Spiritual Exercises), and for this the base of the predication is the subject matter of the first week, in all its meditations, with the examination of conscience and applying the distinct methods of prayer. In regard to the method, generally discursive considerations are also done here; the greater labor continues to pertain to the exercitant. Even though they are of the first week this does not remove the possibility of extending the theme or continuing these Exercises for some days with meditations and documents of the following weeks, that help to reinforce the obtained fruit, to instruct the exercitant and to open the door to further progress49.

62In regards to the application of the Exercises of the first week, there are various possibilities:

a) Exercises of the first week amplified. This is when they are completed with elements of other weeks. Included is the possibility that the Exercises are complete in the themes but partial in the fruits, the latter being in virtue of the dispositions of the exercitant, or of the general impossibility in most cases, by which in few days one reaches the total and complete fruit of the Exercises50. This is what generally happens in the annual exercises (of eight or less days) of priests, religious, seminarians, or lay persons, etc., particularly if they have not previously made the complete Exercises of one month (as such, this cannot be considered as a repetition).

b) Exercises of the first week simplified consist in the complete first week of the Exercises, finishing with the general confession, but adding some additional days for the mild Exercises, namely, to exercise the first method of prayer and the rosary with a meditation of its mysteries.

c) Exercises of the first week intermingled with the light Exercises. This is a combination of the Exercises of the first week with the light Exercises, on account of less complexity or stamina of the person, in such a way that one is only able to make a couple of exercises per day. This follows the scheme of the first week but with only two daily meditations, and to which are added only the Mass and vespers, the first method of prayer for one half-hour, the meditation with the rosary and the examinations.

d) Exercises of the first week spaced out: when occupations impede other things, one is able to apply these Exercises of the first week to the mild form indicated in number [19] of the Book of the Exercises taking in each day only an hour and a half for the exercises.

Fruits

63The first week looks only to the evil, disordered, or imperfect in order to detest and amend it. In this field all are able to work with great profit for the soul, even if they are not disposed to move forward. Even when they make the exercises of the other weeks, but do not aim at a higher end, these can still be called Exercises properly “of the first week” 51. The great leap is to pass from the hatred of evil and all that is disordered to the realm of the good and indifferent, in order to turn the naturally honest loves into spiritual [loves], and to search for and discover that which is most pleasing to the divine majesty52 in particular things, something in a certain sense supererogatory53. This is the complex fruit of the three remaining weeks, which ought to be confronted as such only by one who is disposed to arrive at the end and reach the fruits in all their fullness.

64Nonetheless, the full fruits of the first week are neither few nor without value:

- Inasmuch as one conquers oneself, or subjects reason to God, he obtains the victory over the will and the reform of all deformed concepts: first, with abhorrence of all the sin and disorder of all his life, seeing its intrinsic malice [44]; with the firm determination not to commit mortal sin, venial sin, or any deliberate fault [349], deciding moreover to work seriously on the diminution of semi-deliberate faults and on the amendment of natural defects because of the disorder that all this brings about; with the firm proposition to separate from oneself all that is disordered and worldly because it is irrational and harmful; and with the general proposition to advance each day in perfection, even perhaps without that clear, universal, and effective will of perfection that ratifies a loving and absolute surrender to God so that He freely disposes to His greater glory what pertains more to the complete end of the remaining weeks. The affective dispositions of the will order themselves with the hatred of sin, of the disorder of operations and of the world, set against the love of esteem and returning to the Creator who has preserved me until now, and to the fear of the pains of hell if I am forgetful of the love of God [65]. The generous practice of penance [82-89], together with recollection and silence and the fulfillment of the additions will help the mastery over sensuality.

- In as so far as to regulate one’s life, the subject matter on which one will work does not necessarily regard seeking and finding the divine will, but upon general decisions that the exercitant is already obliged to follow (the Commandments, the Rule, etc). With respect to those decisions, the exercitant will remove from their own conduct all sin and deliberate disorder, and will search for their perfection in the ordinary works that correspond to their proper state of life. For more concrete decisions which regulate one’s life in uncertain matters, not having passed through an election, one can be guided by the counsel of the spiritual director or confessor, and the religious in the instructions of the superiors.

- Touching upon the spiritual formation there are concrete exercises of meditation, and the practice (in the colloquies) of the prayer of supplication. The moral instruction will be more or less according to the knowledge of the exercitant, but certainly formation and refining of the conscience can be given to the exercitant, in addition to what the exercitant will be able to learn so as to understand and fight against scruples and desolation, and will be exercised in the fruitful reception of the sacraments.

When one finishes the exercises of the other weeks, he does not do this searching in a direct way (although it cannot be excluded) to actually obtain the fruit for which he aspires when he makes the complete Exercises, but by means of instruction and trial, in which he sees and considers the true way of perfection and sanctity before God [146], and practically knows the way to arrive at these dispositions [147, 148, 168], having in this way a secure guide in his daily work54.

Persons

65This type of Exercise can be extended to many, all those that have competence, sufficient strength, and a ready will to give oneself to the meditation, spending an entire hour for each exercise; but only aspires to purify the conscience and more or less reform the life that they have already chosen55. Many of these will also be capable of the month-long Exercises, and it is very suitable to awaken in them the desire to do this.

Subject matter

66We have already indicated some things describing the possible forms of the Exercises of the first week: they can follow the scheme of the first week as does the complete Exercises of a month, or reducing them proportionately if one thinks to make an “extended first week” with the other weeks to confirm the established dispositions of the will. In these Exercises it is important to expose in its totality the Principle and Foundation. St. Ignatius indicates that they be given in addition to the stipulated materials “other aids of the exercises of other weeks, the method of prayer and examination of conscience and the like” 56. This looks to secure the fruit of the Exercises for later, by which the exercitants before leaving learn the service of God, set it in their daily lives and continue sustaining the spiritual life, not only persevering but even advancing. For this, St. Ignatius often insists especially to teach the first method of prayer and the general and particular examinations57.

Time

67The indicative times, which can be enlarged or shortened according to suitability or necessity, for each type of Exercise of the first week are: in the case of the extended first week they can be held, in the greatest of dispositions, for eight days or even more with the corresponding days of rest. The ideal is that they are not less than five days. The simplified first week lasts for five to seven days, and the interspersed for three to five days. How they are spread out will be according to the possibility and suitability of the exercitant.

Article 3: The light Exercises

68The difference of the light Exercises in respect to the Exercises of the first week do not rest upon the fruit, but upon the work that the exercitant puts in. As we have said, the first week requires the application of the understanding by means of discursive considerations, which can be a natural incapacity in some persons. The light Exercises, as with the preached exercises, do not require this kind of work from the exercitant.

69The light Exercises58- called thus by St. Ignatius himself- are presented in various forms:

a) The first is in the style of the spaced out Exercises, without abandoning the common obligations, to take only some time of the day for the Exercises. This consists in teaching the first method of prayer (half an hour in the morning), and the third method (in another moment of the day) to make the general and particular examinations, confession, and communion every 8 days or more, and in teaching to conduct oneself well before the movements of the soul in order to discern them.

b) They can also be done in an intensive form, dedicating some days more exclusively to the exercise, until concluding with the general confession.

c) There are light Exercises for children.

d) The principles of the light Exercises can also be combined with those of the preached. We will expound on them later.

Fruits

70We can also call this type of light Exercises catechistic. They already fundamentally consist in bringing the explained catechism to prayer, and through prayer to works.

The fruits that should be produced, following the tripartite scheme applied until now, are:

-With regard to the victory over oneself: repentance from sins committed and the proposition not to deliberately commit neither mortal sin nor venial, nor any fault; the will to correct the sins and deeply rooted defects, by means of particular examination; the general desire to advance each day; and some practice of penance.

- In the regulation of one’s life: “to purify oneself”, in so far as to remove all sin and fault from oneself and learn to practice piety with perfection and fruit.

- In the spiritual formation that is given contains in itself, first, a complete catechetical instruction, geared toward prayer and therefore, it will help form the conscience; second, ascetic, theoretical, and practical instruction: in mental prayer (the first method of prayer, and this each day), in the examination of conscience, in the concrete work against defects and sins (with the particular examination), in praying the vocal prayers with devotion and attention; in the fruitful participation in Holy Mass and the reception of the sacraments, and finally to seek to discern well and learn how to make spiritual direction; third, in the general confession itself with which they conclude.

Persons

71St. Ignatius indicates that “whoever has a will shall be capable of this”. We can note that the light Exercises are proposed for all those that for various limitations are not able to make the Exercises in the discursive way, because of their being coarse, or of a low culture, or in need of basic religious instruction, in which these days there are many. At times it is more advisable to secure the fruit of the minimal religious instruction than to claim fruits which will not be given them [18] due to their lack of this59. Also, this group can include those whom, even being capable, are not disposed nor have the will to make the discursive Exercises, and also those who due to poor health or temperament of the body are not able to bear without great effort an hour of mental prayer, because you cannot give to anyone “things which they could not easily bear” [18].

Subject matter

72In the expression of St. Ignatius himself, this type of the Exercises consists in teaching the service of God, that is, to propose a plan of Christian life and introduce the exercitant to its practice.

One must teach how to apply the first method of prayer regarding the commandments, the precepts of the Church, the capital sins, bodily potencies, and works of mercy [18], giving the doctrine in a half of an hour and leaving that they exercise in this and the other points; to make sure that they know the most important vocal prayers, and so apply the way of prayer by rhythmic breathing in these; that they are able to receive with fruit and regularity the sacraments, knowing well their previous conditions; that they can make the general and particular examinations well in their distinctive times [24-44]; and to give them the elements so that they know to resort to spiritual direction, since it is assumed they will have movements of diverse spirits. Each one of these points ought to be explained pedagogically according to the Catechism, giving the doctrine and basic reasoning, including the talks on the history of salvation, which lay the foundations for and illustrate the truth. Basing a large part of this type of the Exercises in the liturgical prayer, one ought to explain to the exercitants the Mass, its parts, mysteries, and the distinct elements of the liturgy, and the same for the rest of the prayers, etc.

In the intensive form it is advisable to finish with general confession, giving space for the elements that conserve what was gained, confessing more often, and applying the examinations of conscience.

The light Exercises can be completed with some preaching about the eternal truths, by way and themes of popular sermons (for example, those of the popular missions), or by way of adapted readings.

Time

73In its spaced out form (in the midst of normal occupations) it can be proposed to the exercitant to work on this during a month, giving points every so often, in order that the person then continues alone to find spiritual fruit.

In its intensive form it would have to be at least three days, havingPmaterial to stretch it until five or even more days.

Article 4: Preached Exercises

74The preached Exercises60 are those in which he who preaches them does little as a Director and much as a speaker, and those who attend make them in the capacity of listeners, assuming that they do not want or cannot personally exercise oneself. He who preaches them does not indicate nor teach how to use the time given to prayer, nor ask an account of movements, nor strictly “direct” the soul in the development of the Exercises, even when he will be always available for confession and consultation. The preacher has, in a certain way, to supply illustration and conviction for the understanding, the movement of affections, and the persuasion of practical resolutions that the exercitant will have to make for himself in the time of the spiritual exercise. From here comes the importance of the qualities and oratorical preparations of the one who dedicates himself to this, since he should not go to give some points or spiritual themes, but to bring forward a true meditation.

75One can include in this type of Exercises:

a) Popular missions.

b) The open or public Exercises, in churches or parishes (it can be by way of periodic conferences), to more exclusive groups or particular associations.

c) Exercises preached on retreat, or intensive, that should tend to be transformed into light Exercises, or combine with them, or include those which arrive at being transformed into Exercises of the first week or dispose for these.

d) Repetitions, whether for the missions or other manners. The successive repetitions could be spread out at intervals in order to gradually climb until it reaches to be Exercises of the first week, or even more61.

e) Retreat days, in which the first method of prayer with its various subjects and forms constitutes the best way of making the practical examination, the principal exercise of the day62.

76They will be preached Ignatian Exercises in the measure that the themes be taken implicitly or explicitly from the content of the book of the Exercises, inasmuch as they seek to attain a part, the greatest possible, of the total fruit of the complete Exercises; insofar as they tend to convert the listener in the maximum degree that his capacity and state actually permit; and inasmuch as one knows to adapt the focus of the material and the Ignatian scheme to the type of Exercise that is being made, without trying to apply to the letter the strategy proposed in the book of the Exercises, which was intended for the complete Exercises63.

Fruits

77The main objective of the preacher, the fruit that he must seek, is to attain that all who have the capacity and disposition are able to “like and internally feel” the exposed truths, making discursive considerations, making internal actions by themselves in prayer and receiving the divine movements in their potencies, in order to obtain the fullest possible fruit which is proper to the first week, that is, if they do not go further ahead. Or, the preacher must try to convert his listening exercitants.

Considered in itself and in general, the only exposure by means of preaching and non-discursive participation of the listener will bring about at most an actual movement of their feelings, and root up from them a sincere act of the free and elective will, having nonetheless to renounce the fruits of internal and personal work. To cite an example, in reference to the conquest of oneself, one ought to renounce the threefold profound and internal knowledge of their sin, the disorder of their own operations, and the world in them [63] and the corresponding hatreds64. The same principle can be applied to the rest of the fruits that we have signaled as proper to the first week: with preaching alone one will obtain punctual and actual determinations of the will and actual transitory affection, to offend God no longer, and to repent sincerely (which must end with a good confession), with the generic desire to grow and advance in holiness.

As soon as one orders the life, the conscience can be cleaned and educated, and proposes himself to practice piety fruitfully. To him one takes care to regulate the doctrinal and moral instructions with the practical applications that really touch the listeners, “not given “in bulk”, but having in mind the social class and type of audience with whom he meets.

The spiritual formation of the audience must be always present in the intention of the preacher. The sermons must not be directed only to impassion and move the listener, but also to teach by giving them points in order that they can face a serious Christian life. What we have previously indicated about the teaching of the service of God, by means of the methods of prayer and the examinations, is very valuable for them.

Persons

78By what was said, one sees that these preached Exercises have the maximum amplitude of audience, they are directed to all Christians of all states and conditions.

Subject matter

79The subjects are those we have described in the previous types of exercises, dwelling on the subjects of the first week (contemplating the life of Christ, etc.), principally moving towards conversion. Nonetheless, one must keep in mind that in the typical Exercises St. Ignatius rests everything of one’s conversion on the response to the question “what must I do for Christ?” [53], feeling the motive to reciprocate Christ by being grateful enough not to sin. But there will be many who cannot arrive here in a leap, and others who never will arrive. If you presume the case of those who are present, they must be brought step by step to the perfect conversion, beginning with arousing a servile fear of punishment, in order to bring about later a shame for the sins they have committed and the pain of losing heaven, in order to secure contrition and with it a valid sacramental confession. Afterwards, this will bring about perfect contrition.

Article 5: The new evangelization

80We consider that the Spiritual Exercises of St. Ignatius constitute one of the most efficacious instruments to bring forward the new evangelization to which the Holy Father summons us, “new in its vigor, in its methods, in its expression”65.

81It is among the most efficacious instruments because it essentially aims at conversion, to the metanoia (Mt 3:2, 4:17; Mk 1:15; Acts 2:38; 3:19). If it is well used, it is a valid instrument for the new evangelization despite that it is more than 400 years old, because as the Holy Father said, "it will be new in its ardor, if as it is opened you corroborate more and more with the union with Christ, the first evangelist… it will be new in its methods if each of the members of the Church become protagonists of the spreading of the message of Christ… it order that it will be new also in its expression you must be with ears attentive to what the Lord says, this is always in an attitude of listening to what the Lord himself can suggest in any moment66. New Evangelization, that is a “fascinating adventure”67, “arduous and exciting68, calls us all.

In relation to the new methods of evangelization, as well as for preaching the spiritual exercises, all modern means of communication can and must be used. For example, the spiritual exercises can be preached with much fruit by the internet, with great interaction on the part of the virtual exercitant, and in different manners. One form to have in mind is the annotation [19], preaching the exercises by internet to people who are not able to leave their daily jobs. Another way is to invite exercitants to dedicate some days (at least 3) in a place where they can be without their occupations and with enough tranquility to complete a schedule similar to that of a spiritual exercise "in person”69.
