Chapter 2: Glossary of the Exercises according to Fr. Calveras

95We present now in alphabetical order a glossary of the most important words used by St. Ignatius, or “index words”, following Fr. Calveras93. It is a top-line instrument in the intelligence of the Exercises, and therefore an aid of great importance for those who “give” them, seeing that it permits a transversal and organic reading of the work of St. Ignatius. It reveals in all its profundity the value and weight of the “power ideas”.

96. Affection

I. In general

a) Particular love towards a person or thing, with the interest to favor or have it [16, 150, 184, 338, 342].

b) This interest, born from affection inclines toward a person or thing [155], or toward self-love and self-interest [157, 166].

II. Disordered

When such love or interest is not purely for God [1, 16, 21, 150, 169, 172, 184, 338], they ought to remove or rightly order all interests, before seeking the divine will, when it is not clear [1, 16, 157, 342]; it is the work of God to change an affection, ordering the desires [16]; we are to prepare ourselves, asking for this in prayer [16], and disposing ourselves to be determined to leave aside what interests us, if God so desires it [154], and even inclining ourselves to this [155], and asking that God grant it to be such [157].

97. To Affect

1. Act. and refl. To stir the affections [50, 363], we use the acts of the affective will [3], endeavoring to make myself (affect=rouse the emotions) rejoice with the joy and happiness of Christ [229]; as one makes an offering with deep affection [234] (=with growth [60], with great affection [234]).

2. To aspire: to receive the Blessed Sacrament every 15 days, and if one is so moved, better every eight days [18], those who want to affect more [97].

3. To feel or have an inclination toward something [157]; I do not desire nor do I feel strongly attached to having riches rather than poverty [166]; am not more inclined or emotionally disposed toward taking a thing or leaving it [179]; if one is moved by affection in searching for an office [16]; if such a soul is affected and inclined inordinately toward a thing [16] (=attached) [338, 342]; for man to be lovingly attached to the true doctrine of Christ [164].

4. To be well or poorly disposed: to overcome the affection toward that to which one is wrongly attached, one must bring oneself to desire its contrary [16].

98. Affection

1. Equivalent to an affection [153, 155, 157]; disordered [153, 154, 155, 157].

2. Feeling: to stir up affections [50], is more proper to positive doctors [363], with surging emotion [60], with much affection [234].

3. Disposition of the will: as far as the affections are concerned one gives up everything [155].

99. Help

1. To serve, to be of use for something [23, 44, 65, 91, 130, 169, 229, 345, 370]; to make possible, easy [72, 177, 205].

2. Active verb: To facilitate another [41, 146].

3. Pron. Of profitable use [363].

100. To help oneself

1. To play your part, to cooperate: the angels, not wanting to help with their liberty to revere and obey their Creator, were converted from grace into wickedness [50]; annotations to help oneself, for the one who has to give the Exercises and as for those who have to receive them [1]; so that one and likewise others are better helped and profit to strive to save his neighbor’s proposition [22]; the Exercises are to be given so that each one according to his wish to dispose himself, no longer proposes more of what they want, because in this they will help themselves, will work and will profit; so to him alone who wants to help himself to be instructed and come to a certain degree of contentment of soul, making it precisely in order to save himself [18].

2. To prepare and dispose oneself: all ways of preparing and disposing the soul in order to remove from it all disordered affections [1]; one prepares by asking the grace, asking in prayer to God the contrary, that the ordering of desires changes the disordered affection into ordered affection [16]; one is disposed instantly in other spiritual exercises with the will to the contrary, in which he does not want this nor some other thing, unless he is moved only in the service of God [155], once He changes the his first affection for him [16]; making one prepared and disposed to the chance consolation [7]; placing one’s endeavors against desolation, and hoping that soon he will be consoled [321]; the endeavors are to insist more in prayer and in the colloquies (to prepare oneself), to lengthen the meditation, to examine oneself much ascertaining the cause, to prolong in some suitable way the performance of penance (to dispose oneself) [319]; for the hours of the exercises we prepare ourselves with the preparatory prayer at the beginning of each, begging the grace to obtain the general fruit of all the Exercises, and we emphasize in the last prelude, asking the grace of a particular fruit of each exercise; and we dispose ourselves proximately and remotely with the safeguard of the additions, especially with the examination of the exercise, that searches for the cause of that which went wrong, in order to remove it immediately, and to give thanks to God, if I have done well, and proceed in the same manner [77]; with the solitude and silence, discovering the soul more alone and isolated makes one more apt to approach and reach its Creator, and the more it so approaches Him, the more it disposes itself to receive graces and gifts from His Divine Goodness [20]; we assist with penance, which makes one to search and discover some grace or gift that the person wants and desires [87]; the two standards teaches one how we ought to dispose in order to come to perfection in any state of life [135]; namely, for the utmost spiritual poverty, the desire for reproaches and contempt, and humility, and from these three steps to all other virtues [146]; those who are perfect contemplate more the being of God Our Lord in each creature, and are disposed to esteem and revere their Creator [39].

3. To ready oneself: with the general confession at the end of the first week being better confessed and disposed, discovers himself to be more apt and readied to receive the Holy Eucharist [44]; the first method of prayer are exercises how the soul readies itself and profits by them, and that the prayer may be more acceptable (it disposes him and with this advance in virtue, and making him more agreeable to God, by which the prayer is more accepted) [238].

101. Colloquy

1. When to make one: at the end of all meditations [53, 61, 63, 71, 147, 156], at the end of all contemplations [109, 117, 118, 126, 159, 198, 199, 225, 237], in the consideration of the three ways of humility throughout the whole day [164, 168], upon finishing the first and second methods of prayer [243, 244, 246, 257]; or to God [61, 237, 243, 244, 246], and Christ [53, 71, 198, 199, 225], or speaking to the three divine persons, to the Incarnate Word and to the Blessed Virgin [109, 117, 118, 120, 126], or to the person to whom you have spoken [257], or three to Our Lady, to the Son, and to the Father [63, 147, 156, 159, 199, 225]. The three colloquies of the classes of men can be reinforced with the following note [199]. Conclude without colloquy, with an offering to the temporal king [98], and the ways of making an election [183, 188]. Without any other particular thing, the particular examination [25], and the general examination [43], and the third method of prayer [258].

2. How to do one: properly it is made speaking [54, 109], or reasoning [61, 199], discoursing about what to offer Him [53], a servant to the Lord, or a friend to a friend, blaming oneself for any wrong done [54], and proposing amendments with grace [61]; giving thanks for such pity and mercy that He has had with me, not ending my life [61, 71]; and asking according as I find myself tempted or consoled, or I want to grieve or rejoice at the thing contemplated; as I want to have one virtue or another [199], asking for some grace [54, 63], the virtues or graces of which I feel to be of greatest need [257], that which I more efficaciously desire as to any particular things [199], or in order to follow Christ more closely [109, 147, 156, 157, 159, 168]. In short communicating one’s affairs and asking advice in them [54], according as I want to dispose of myself in one direction or another [199], according to the subject matter or actual disposition [199, 225]; the devotion will move me to one or three colloquies [199], in offerings ask that He may accept them [183, 188], and confide in the aid of God to complete them [98]; ask forgiveness and pardon from faults in the general examination [43], and in each commandment, sin, etc., in the first method of prayer [241], after accusing myself of each [243].

102. Christ

I. Names and titles

In the text, he is called Christ 40 times, Christ Our Lord 71 times, Jesus Christ [only once 47]; Jesus 22 times (of these 7 times Child Jesus, Jesus the Galilean [294], and Jesus of Nazareth [300]); also 4 times as the Child [265, 266, 269, 270].

Jesus: once Creator [35] and Creator and Redeemer [229]; 19 the Lord, once the Eternal Lord [65] 10 Lord (universal Lord [97]); once Eternal Lord [98]; once God: my Lord and my God [305]; twice he is designated Eternal Word Incarnate [109, 130]; 7 Son in respect to the Father, and in relation to Mary 4 times her Son and 3 her Son and Lord; surnamed Infinite Goodness [98], Most Holy [98], Divine Majesty [248], King Eternal [91], eternal [95, 97], of the Jews [295, 296]; Son of God [274], of David [287], of man [284]; Savior of the world [265]; our Commander-in-chief and Lord [136], supreme Commander-in-chief of the good [138], supreme and true Captain [139]; High Priest, our model and rule [344]; Bridegroom [365] with respect to the Church, His true Bride [353, 365]; and finally he is compared to a friend who advises another [224].

II. The Conduct of Christ

He is presented in the Exercises:

a) As Redeemer: from the Creator he is sent to become man and from eternal life to temporal death and likewise to die for my sins [53]; all that he suffers in the passion he suffers for my sins [197]; that He has not left me to fall into any of the divisions of the condemned, ending my life [71].

b) King and Captain, that goes in front in the conquest of all the enemies, especially in the war against carnal, sensual, and worldly love [95, 116], embracing poverty, humiliations, and sufferings, from Bethlehem until Calvary for me [116], to make the cross of the perfect accomplishment of the divine will more bearable [91, 95].

c) Model, to copy, reflecting on Him after considering His person, words, and works [114, 116], in order to order oneself in deed [63], in eating [214], in the use of the senses [248], in what is proper to the person and state [344].

d) Friend, with whom in the colloquies one communicates their affairs and asks council in them [54, 199]; of whom one awaits consolation [224, 234]; with whom one is intimate in the contemplation of his life, until feeling his sufferings as one’s own [203, 206] and his joy and happiness [221, 229]; that has for friends the servants that were sent throughout all the world [146]; his beloved disciples [278, 281, 284].

III. That’s why the exercitant

a) Has to know Him intimately: considering His divine person, always seeing in Him the Eternal Word Incarnate [109, 130], the Creator [53], the Lord who was made man for him [104]; His divinity: after considering the divine attributes, comparing them to their contraries in himself [59], smelling and tasting His infinite fragrance and sweetness in the work of the senses [124]; seeing as in the actual passion, not destroying the enemies and leaving the humanity to suffer so cruelly [196], how it remains united to the body and soul of Christ after His death [219], and how it is manifested so miraculously in the resurrection [223]; His humanity, seeing it and watching it in all the mysteries of his life, passion, and resurrection [114], meditating and contemplating in particular His circumstances [122], hearing, noticing, and contemplating what He says or can say [115, 123], smelling and tasting the fragrance of His soul, His virtues, and all things [124]; His true doctrine [164], that surrounds the true life of the spirit [139] to know, by the supreme spiritual poverty, and by the desire for humiliations, to arrive at humility or full subjection to God, and by these three steps to ascend to all other virtues [146] in order to come to the perfection each one in his well chosen state [135]; His work: the constant war from the manger to the cross against carnal love, sensual and worldly, born in the greatest poverty, and as the end of so many labors- of hunger, thirst, heat and cold, injuries and affronts- to die on the cross and all this for me[116]; and the cost of my redemption, how many and which things and with what love, taking part divinity and humanity, he suffered for my sins[53, 193, 197]; contemplating through this what he suffers in His humanity in each step of the passion [195, 196], making a repetition of all this until the end [208], and frequently bringing to memory the labors, fatigue and pains that He suffered from the point of His birth until the present mystery [206]

b) To love Him with a growing love [104], in return, responding generously to the question, what ought I to do and suffer for Him [53, 197], to know, to avoid all sin and voluntary faults [63, 349], to surrender oneself entirely to do always what is most pleasing to God [151], quick and diligent to do His will [91]; for this end disposed to embrace poverty and not evade humiliations [167] and sufferings, so long as it is not contrary to the greater glory of God [167]; of esteem, forming a high concept of His divine and human perfections [104]; of intimacy with continual intercourse, as if present he finds me [114], until feeling the pains of His passion as my own [48, 203, 206] and the joys of the resurrection [221, 229], reinforcing with love, effect of the consolation (tears moved to love of your Lord by the passion [316]); with which he prepares the soul to establish a life of formal friendship with God [234].

c) To imitate Him, serve Him, and follow Him: taking Him as a model, to copy His ways; to serve Him in His necessities with all esteem and reverence in the contemplation of His mysteries, as finding Him present in spirit [114]; and by demonstration of a special affection toward His person, to offer oneself for what is the most difficult against the inclination of sensuality, flesh, and the world [98]; and in fact to embrace it, so long as it is not opposed to the greatest divine service [167], following Him likewise in pain [95, 109, 130], in order to follow Him later in glory [95].

103. God

I. Considered in Himself

1. One God, names and titles: in the text the Word God alone appears 25 times, 58 times he says God our Lord, once Our God and Lord [343]; 8 times Creator [15, 20, 38, 39, 316, 330], 16 times Creator and Lord [5, 15, 16, 20, 38, 39, 50, 52, 184, 316, 317, 324, 351]; once Lord and Creator [39]; 12 times the Lord [157, 177, 234, 263, 265, 268, 287, 290, 316, 320, 362]; once the Eternal Lord [63]; 3 times Lord (vocative) [234, 268]; he calls God Infinite Goodness [52], Divine Goodness [20, 151, 157]; and 23 times Divine Majesty.

2. Triune God:

a) The Trinity: the three divine persons looked at all the plains of all the earth full of men; determined that the second person would become man [102]; to consider the three divine persons, how they look at all the peoples in such blindness [106]; to hear what the three divine persons say [107]; to look at what they do [108]; to make a colloquy, thinking what I ought to say to the three divine persons, or to the Word Incarnate, or to Our Mother [109].

b) The persons: baptizing them in the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit [307]; the Father 14 times named Father, once eternal Father [135], and giving the title the eternal Lord [63]; the Son: 7 times named in respect to the Father, twice Eternal Word incarnate [109, 130]; the Holy Spirit: likewise 6 times, once Spirit and our Lord [365].

II. His communication with the creature

In the Exercises, it is much better that the Creator communicates himself with the soul, and the one who [gives the Exercises] should allow the Creator to work immediately on the creature and the creature with his Creator.

1. Work of God: God works in the soul manifestly, when He visits it with His gifts and spiritual graces; in a hidden manner, when, with an unperceived grace, which anticipates and accompanies the exercise of the natural faculties in order to practice acts of virtue and resist temptations:

a) Manifest action: (gifts and graces): in consolations without preceding cause the Lord himself works immediately in the will, inflaming the soul in the love of His majesty, and ordering the love of creatures, in such a way that no creature is loved in itself except for the Creator [316,440]; and when one wants to discover immediately His will, one moves thus and attracts the human will, that the soul without doubt nor being able to doubt follows what has been shown to it [175], and in this time he gives understanding of other things, in which one is not able to be deceived, by being from God alone; although one can have this in the following time [336]; with preceding cause previous knowledge or sentiment of some object, consolation can come mediated by acts of understanding and will through the work of the good angel or evil spirit [330]; the consolations of God and His angels always give true gladness and spiritual joy, and not the pretenses of the evil spirit [329] that end in what is evil, less good, or distracting, or destroy the good effects of the consolation [333]; of the inferior order they are spiritual graces, effect of the exercise of our faculties with the concurrence of an intense grace [320], such as knowledge, feelings, favors, devotion, that we search for in the diverse exercises [62, 118, 227, 252, 254], with which grace it is easy to resist the enemy[323, 324]; the Lord at times abstracts consolations and intense grace from the soul and leaves it in desolation with sufficient hidden grace, at that time He allows the enemy to assail it with temptations and agitate and vex it with sadness and distress, in order to test its fidelity [320, 321]; and as in the time of desolation the evil spirit acts freely, likewise that of consolation one is left to feel the good spirit with inspirations and other good effects [315, 317, 318]; by means of movements in the will in the time of consolation with cause and desolation and of the action of various spirits, many times God gives direct understanding of His will, and this can be evident to us when one reaches sufficient clarity and knowledge, examining the movements and the spirits[176].

b) Hidden action: with the diligent exercise of our natural potencies, readied and aided by hidden grace, we have to work to reach the proposed fruit, when we are not favored by intense grace or consolation, nor experience the movement of the spirits; in these circumstances we are able to know the divine will indirectly, taking as such that which by natural judgment, aided by grace, appears more conformed to the divine service [180-182], and even that to which we are inclined by love manifestly spiritual [184, 338, 342], after having sincerely offered this to God and having prayed to confirm this, if it is of His greater service and praise[183, 188]; the grace, which we have counted on for everything, has to be asked for from the beginning, and in turn we ought to give thanks that He helps us.

c) Importance of the evident action: the spiritual graces fully contain the fruit of the Exercises in themselves; the gifts perfect it, reinforcing the graces [87, 316]; and with the increase of theological virtues that they bring, and with the interior joy that calls and attracts toward celestial things [316], they detach the heart from creatures, so as not to love anything but God, and with this it orders the desires to God, in that all disordered loves or affections toward persons and things become ordered [1, 16], and the love of ourselves [189], the most principal part of all of this regarding the victory over ourselves; the internal movements of consolation and desolation and the movement of different spirits assume in the exercitant that he makes in his course and does well the exercises and guards with diligence the additions [6]; and in the repetitions there is to be a pause where one has felt the spiritual graces and consolation or desolation [62, 118, 227, 252, 254].

2. Work of the creature: in order to receive gifts and graces from the divine and supreme goodness [20], aside from the immediate preparation of supplications in the preludes and colloquies, and of corporal penances [87, 89], it is worthwhile to dispose ourselves [20]:

a) making ourselves pleasing to God, with the diligent employment of our natural faculties in the exercises [3, 20, 117], to clean ourselves of sin and voluntary faults [63, 349], amend the disorder of the operations [63], order and perfect works [63];

b) compelling Him with liberality, offering Him all our desires and liberty, that He dispose of us and of all that is ours in conformity with His will [5]; not contenting ourselves with the offering of all our being to the work with Christ, but wanting to mark ourselves in His service, making oblations in order to imitate Him in undergoing humiliations and poverty [98], urging that such an offering may be realized, with petitions to be received under His standard in actual poverty and in suffering injuries so in these to imitate Him better [147], and asking that He would be pleased to choose us in the 3rd greatest and best humility [168]; until finishing with the absolute surrender to God of all our liberty with all that we are and possess, that disposes all according to His will [234]; the sincerity, looking straight to the end of doing what is more pleasing to God, in which we will choose (life or state, if it is appropriate; reform of one’s own life and state [174, 189]), not ordering nor bringing the end to the means, wanting that God comes to what is more suitable to us [154, 169], but the means to the end, disposed to leave what we have, if God is more pleased, and looking solely to the end with the simple eye of the intention, only attending to the divine service [16, 155, 169, 181, 182], going out entirely from our own love, desire and interest, in order to take advantage in every way possible [169, 189]; and the generous fidelity in making the exercises, because being in tepidity, laziness, or negligence distances us from spiritual consolation [322] (to prepare them [228], well completed hour [12,13], additions, especially the fifth, a quarter of an hour of examination until discovering the cause [77]); in resisting temptations in time of desolation, in which the Lord has put us to the test, in order to see how much we are and how much we let ourselves out of His service without His intense grace and consolation [322], not remaining on the defense, but making a counter (per diametrum) against the enemy [13, 217, 325, 350, 351]; and not only working to be patient in the vexations that come from sadness and disturbance[321], and without changing resolutions [318], but intensely changing ourselves against the same desolation, as by insisting on more prayer and meditation, frequent examination of the causes and some suitable increase in penance [319, 321]; and in the same consolation, giving thanks to God [77], and attributing it to Him and not to ourselves [322, 324]; taking advantage, thinking of the desolation that will come, taking new strength for then, in which we will experience again how little we are [322, 324]; and pursuing the manner to proceed that we have valued the consolation [77]; in giving faithful account to the director of the thoughts and various agitations that the spirits bring [17, 326]; and finally to faithfully complete what we have known clearly to be the will of God[366];

c) Removing internal obstacles: extinguishing all repugnance or affect against poverty or other things of perfection [157], and in fact ordering, putting all one’s strength into this [16], all love and particular affection for persons and things [1, 16,150, 155, 184, 338]; so as to be able to find God in the peace of soul, for the particular affection toward an acquired thing is a grave or heavy hindrance [150, 153], and in order to receive more certainly, without danger of deception, the direct manifestation of that which the Creator desires from us [16]; and the external impediments, separating us from friends and acquaintances, and from all earthly concerns in affairs not well-ordered (7th, 8th, and 9th additions), with interior serenity we are able to draw near more freely to God, drawing closer to dispose ourselves to receive graces and gifts from Him [20];

d) inducing those internal dispositions that are more in harmony with the graces and gifts that we desire to reach, governing our thoughts within the day, especially upon waking (1st, 2nd, and 6th addition) - [5, 17, 20, 77, 89, 150, 319, 321, 324, 327, 336].

III. Communication of mutual friendship

In the contemplation of love one strikes up a formal friendship of the soul with God, mediating the perfect exchange of all one’s things and with them of one’s own self, in return for the abundance that God has given and done for him, and desires to give himself insofar as he is able [234]; to take with him from the Exercises a life of communication with God principally in works and also in words [230, 231] from our part; and God on His own, with His gifts and spiritual graces visits us [20, 234].

1. Communication of works:

a) The soul has to continue making itself each time more grateful to God, perfecting his works more each day, so that he values the frequent practice of the first method of prayer with its various subject matters [238-248], which constitute a fitting exercise in order to ready oneself and profit, so that this prayer may be acceptable [237]; procuring the acquisition and conservation of the seven virtues contrary to the mortal sins with holy exercises [245]; and stocking oneself well with virtues, theological, cardinal, and moral, so that the enemy does not find a weak spot by which to take us [327]; each one perfecting himself in his proper state or life in as much as he is able [173], to come to perfection [135]; because being the soul created in the image and likeness of God, it touches the divine honor, that it may be neither dirty nor disordered, but more beautiful and perfect [235];

b) It has to employ its energies and resources, that it has surrendered entirely to God, after the work of its own sanctification, in the faithful discharge of its duty, occupation, and obligations of state or life, that by sincere obedience or upright election it has taken, aspiring that noteworthy and very affable fruits go forth to God [174], always prompt and diligent to complete any indication of the divine will [91], and to accept with acts of thanksgiving that which the Lord disposes or permits, even mortification, thinking that they serve Him not only by doing but also, and even more so, by suffering [53, 197];

c) Considering how God works for the soul through all created things on the face of the earth, thinking of it when He gathers together the effects of creatures that the soul has to make use of [236], the soul works through God in all that it does, seeking solely to please Him by the benefits received [234], by the love with which all is disposed to His good [236]; and by being Him in himself most worthy of all service [237]; serving Him much through pure love [370], even helping oneself out of servile fear [65, 370]. [56, 157, 230]

2. Communication of words:

a) In the exercises of piety, seeking intimacy with God and the saints in mental prayer, the points prepared with diligence [228], speaking and asking with total reverence [3, 54, 199]; after placing oneself in the presence of God [75, 151, 232]; joining mental and vocal prayer in the recitation of prayers [1], making use of the 2nd and 3rd methods of prayer [240, 258, 260];

b) In the presence of God throughout the day, looking for God in all things and within myself, as well as in all in whom He dwells and in myself [235], making it a habit with the assiduous contemplation of the understanding, aided by divine illumination, to consider, meditate and contemplate, as the perfect, the being of God in each creature, according to His proper essence, presence and power [39]; perceiving my constant dependency on God in each work [235], presenting myself to the principle of all action in order to ask His help [25], wanting to follow His direction in all things for the highest spiritual good [174]; raising ones thoughts to God during temptations and needs [351]; renewing ones intention in works, pleasing myself to work for God, who works for me in all things [236]; making this to resound in my soul, which is the temple of God [235], praises for all my goods and those of others that I discover [237], attributing them to Him [322]; and acts of thanksgiving for the resulting goods and continuous benefits [43, 77];

c) Giving place to dialogue, in which God speaks with the communication of His graces and gifts, that we have asked in return for our full surrender of ourselves [234]; keeping the soul in peace, without the disturbance of actual repugnancies or affects, and of disordered love toward any person or thing [16, 150, 157], and free in the midst of ordered occupations [20], able to hear God always and in all parts; and strengthened with fidelity in not searching for nor allowing any creature to give consolation to satisfy the heart, but only God [224]; then to ask that He give us His love and grace in return, we have protested in order to oblige Him, for only this is enough for us [234]; keeping watch especially in time of desolation when we feel the movement toward low and earthly things, responding with prayer, meditation, examining the cause, and doing more penance [319], in order to provoke the prompt return of consolation[321].

3. Concentration of every love in God:

a) The communication of works and words must be a manifestation of true love of God concentrated in the heart, when by intimate knowledge of the infinite divine perfections and by experience of His internal communications in such a way, we are enamored by the Lord, that the value of the limited perfections which He has parceled out to creatures almost disappears, and likewise our full complacency and benevolence cannot rest but in the infinite goodness of God, separating oneself as far as possible from the love of all creatures so as to place this love in their Creator [273], to which knowledge and love of Christ, of His humanity and His divinity, has been prepared for us.

III. Movement

1. Rational and sensitive: that which reason says or nature inclines to [182].

2. Towards base and earthly things: attracted by things of the world, type of desolation, opposed to interior joy, that summons and draws man toward heavenly things [316, 317].

3. Interior movement: that which is caused interiorly in the soul [313] by the work of God Himself or from the good or evil spirits [329-331].

I. Forms:

a) Consolation, all gratuitous gifts from God, which are not in our power to bring about or possess [322], that which He gives either with a preceding cause, prior awareness or knowledge of some object, by which the said consolation comes through acts of the intellect and will [330], and could be the work of the good angel or of the evil one for contrary ends [331], or without such a cause it is the work of God alone, whose prerogative it is to come into and leave the soul in order to directly move the soul [330];

b) Desolation, when God withdraws from the soul the consolation and extraordinary graces, testing it by leaving it to its own natural powers, with only sufficient hidden grace to resist the diverse tribulations and temptations of the enemy [320].

II. General Characteristics:

a) Consolation, as the gift that it is, is distinguished from spiritual graces: with solitude and silence the soul draws nearer to God and disposes itself to receive graces and gifts from His Divine Goodness [20]; penances are performed to seek and find some grace or gift [87]; in as far as we are able to advance in His service without the reward of such consolations or increase of graces [322], how little the soul is in time of desolation without such grace or consolation [324]; in the repetitions and the second way of prayer contrasting movements occur, consolation and desolation in the understanding, feelings, likes, tastes which are spiritual graces [62, 118, 204, 227, 252, 254];

b). Movements are also distinguished from the agitations of the diverse spirits: when the exercitant does not have any spiritual movements in his soul, like consolations or desolations, nor is he agitated by different spirits [6]; when the mind is quite clear and deriving its knowledge from previous experience of comfort or distress, and is versed in discrimination of different spirits [176];

c) The interference of different spirits in movements: temptations and agitation of spirits involved in desolation, in which the soul is agitated or tested by different spirits [4, 320]; interior lights and inspirations [213] of the good spirit [315] with consolations [213, 315]: just as consolation is contrary to desolation, so too, the thoughts produced by the former are contrary to those of the latter [317]; in consolation the good spirit guides and counsels us, but in desolation the evil spirit, by whose counsels we can never find the way to a right decision [318]; furthermore after such an occasion without cause, we form convictions and resolutions based on the good spirit or on the evil one, in which, since these do not come immediately from God, we can be deceived [336];

d) Time of consolation and desolation: One should distinguish the time when the consolation itself was present from the time after it, in which the soul remains still warm and favored with the gifts and aftereffects of the consolation which has itself passed away [336]; likewise in desolation the actual work of the spirits, of the effects which it leaves and of the privation of consolation and intense grace [320, 321]; it is important to perceive or be aware of all such activity that arises in the soul, and know to discern the good from the ill in order to receive or reject it [313].

III. Consolation, to console

1. Unitive:

a) Forms: to inflame the soul with love of its Creator [316], even without preceding cause, because it is proper of the Creator to cause a motion in the soul which draws the whole person into the love of His Divine Majesty [330], intense love [322], sufficient [320]; the soul can love no created thing on the face of the earth in itself, but only in the Creator of them all [316]; tears move one to love, out of sorrow for one’s own sins, or for the passion of Our Lord or other spiritual motives [316]; increase of hope, faith and charity [316], with increased devotion [322]; interior joy, which calls and attracts one toward heavenly things and to the salvation of one’s soul [316]; divine help clearly perceived [320];

b) Effects: the soul in effect is left warm and favored with the gifts (fervor) and aftereffects of the past consolation [336], abundant fervor [14, 320], happiness [329] and spiritual joy [329, 334], gentleness [124, 334], sweetness [124], peace [150, 153, 333], tranquility [333] and stillness [315, 334], silencing and pacifying the soul with its Creator and Lord [150, 153,316];

c) Intervention of the good spirit in times of consolation, giving courage and strength, with internal lights and inspirations.

2. Elective: movement or attraction of the will to what God proposes, in such a way that it is without doubt nor is it able to doubt [175], without preceding cause, and without possibility of deceit, since it is from God alone [336]; movement or inclination of the will until a point in a consolation with preceding cause [176], by the good spirit or the evil one [331].

3. False consolation: in acts of the understanding and of the will, without any previous perception or understanding of some object, the evil spirit can produce movements in the soul similar to those worked by God and His angels [329, 330, 331], not for the benefit of the soul, that it may grow and rise from what is good to what is better, but for the contrary purpose, to entice the soul to what is evil [331, 333]; these never effect a genuine happiness and spiritual joy, because the enemy is fighting against these, introducing sadness and distress [329].

IV. Desolation, desolate:

a) Forms: darkness of the soul, turmoil within it, in impulsive motion toward low and earthly things or disquiet from various agitations and temptations, moving it toward a lack of faith, a lack of hope in what was said above [317], a loss of augmented love [320], without love [317].

b) Effects: without fervor [320], finding itself completely listless, tepid, and unhappy, and feels separated from God [317], without peace, disturbed [317, 329, 333]; in desolation more often the evil spirit guides and counsels us [318], testing the soul with temptations, especially against faith and hope [317], and vexes it with sadness and turmoil [4, 321, 329];

c) Causes of desolation: there are three chief causes: our neglect of the spiritual exercises, to test how much we are worth and how far we will extend ourselves for God without consolation or intense graces, to prevent arrogance and vainglory, making us perceive that we are capable of nothing outside consolation, and that everything must be attributed to God [322].

V. Our Conduct:

In the Exercises, consolations are desired [87, 89], sought with penance [87], making a change in this when consolations fail to come [89], and assuming that they will be felt, especially in the hours of the exercises but also in the repetitions one must emphasize the points or principle parts where these were felt [62, 18, 227]:

a) Prepare and dispose ourselves for consolation: fidelity to the spiritual exercises, since by being tepid, lazy, or negligent in these we distance consolation from ourselves [322]; in time of consolation it is easy and scarcely taxing to remain in contemplation for a full hour, but in time of desolation it is very difficult to complete this time [13]; in solitude and silence the soul draws nearer to God and disposes itself to receive graces and gifts from His divine goodness [20]; in supplication and colloquies [199, 319], and with bodily penance we compel God, seeking the gift or grace which we desire [87], and making some change in this when God delays His favors; to give thanks for gifts received [77], faithfully attributing them to God [322];

b) In time of consolation: one who is in consolation should consider how he will act in future desolation, and store up strength for that time [323]; seeking to humble and abase himself as much as possible, and reflect how little he is worth in time of desolation when that grace or consolation is absent [324]; examine the consolation with the rules for discernment of spirits, the action of the spirits, the propositions and train of thought, in order to free oneself from all deceit [333-336]; seek to proceed in the same manner, as seen in by the examination of the exercise, that led to consolation [77];

c) In time of desolation: counter it with an increase of prayer [319] and colloquies [199], with more meditation and examination [319], searching for its cause among those given in the Exercises [322], and finding it, repent and remove it [77], insisting more on penance [319]; work to be patient in the trials that come, and consider that soon consolation will follow [321], prepare and dispose yourself for this [7], make diligent efforts against it, as said [321]; do not change your resolutions or determinations made the day before or in the previous consolation [318]; do not fear, nor lose courage in suffering temptations [325], and draw strength in your Creator, thinking that He can do much with the hidden graces which always remain [320, 324]; consider how the Lord has left you with your own natural powers, testing your resistance to the different tribulations and temptations of the enemy [320]; and He wants to test how far you are willing to extend yourself in His service, without the aid of such consolations and augmented graces [322], if you please Him by resisting or if you will overthrow the adversary [13], doing the opposite per diámetrum [325]; with desolate and tempted exercitants the director should be mild and gentle, giving courage and strength, uncovering the astuteness of the enemy and having him work so as to be newly consoled [7];

d) In elections: be attentive if the Lord moves and attracts the will as proper to the first time suitable for an election [175]; if not the case, examine the movements of consolations which proceed from cause, movements of desolation, and the work of the spirits, so that in the second time you can have the greatest clarity possible through your experience of consolation, desolation, and discernment of spirits [176], or in the third suitable time, in a period of tranquility [177].

114To Order one’s Life

I. Subject matter:

Life or state and manner of living [15, 177], ecclesiastical office or benefice [16, 171], temporal goods [171], house and family [189], what is worldly and vain [63]; all my intentions, actions and operations (all my desires, aspirations and particular resolutions, which constitute my intentions; and all of my works, both with others, in exterior occupations or actions, and within myself, in my spiritual, intellectual, and physical responsibilities of my personal life or operations) [46, 63]; the general will to avoid all that is evil or disordered and to always do what is more pleasing to God, and to change the affective dispositions of the will, and ordering love, all refer to victory over oneself.

II. Norms of Order:

Not only to avoid grave and venial sin, but to avoid all disorder [63], weighing all things, not if they are commanded or prohibited, but insofar as they better conform to our final end, the glory of God and our sanctification [23]; to make use of things insofar as they help man to his end, that is, proceeding in all things according to what is justly and purely for the Divine service [16, 150, 155, 169, 172, 173, 177, 179, 181, 184, 189, 233, 234, 236, 338], and choosing in each case what is more conducive to this end [23, 185, 189, 339], that which gives greater glory and praise to God [179, 180, 185]; to concur always with what is more pleasing to Divine Goodness [151], with the most holy will of God [180], which prohibits disorders against reason under weight of mortal or venial sin, and with threat of eternal or temporary punishment, according to their degree [23, 35, 41, 52, 53, 57, 193, 197]; disapproval of all faults and imperfections, since our faults keep consolation from us [322], and of these we must ask pardon and forgiveness [43, 241]; and inciting us to all perfection: for the highest degree of poverty and a desire of reproaches and contempt since it results in humility, and from these three steps all other virtues [146]; to give inspirations is from the good spirit, and to remove all obstacles so that in good works one may proceed forward [315], as are consolations, in order to cause the soul to grow and rise from what is good to what is better [331]; in whichever state of life we choose, we must come to perfection by the way of humility [135]; and in the election well made we must perfect ourselves as much as possible [173]; in the external practice of virtues (actual poverty and humiliations) an increase in these is not always the greatest divine service [98, 146, 147, 157, 167, 168]; and in the means of perfection, especially in the following of the common state of keeping the commandments, or in the state of evangelical perfection [135], God indicates to each one the way in which they will better serve Him [15, 343].

III. Progressive Steps:

a) To cleanse oneself [32] of all mortal and venial sin, and all fully deliberate faults [35-37, 165, 166, 348, 349, 370];

b) To amend one’s disordered operations and Works [63] (defects, even those rooted in one’s personality or habits [24-27], negligence [35, 90, 160], semi-deliberate faults [160]), and to rid oneself from all that is worldly and vain (dress, apparel) [63];

c) To order oneself, doing ordinary tasks with perfection, observing the additions of the exercises [73-88], of the particular examination [27-30], the rules for eating [210-217], for almsgiving [337-344];

d) To store up virtues, theological, cardinal, and moral, so the enemy does not find a weak spot whereby to attack and take us [327], and especially with holy exercises, seek to acquire and conserve the seven virtues contrary to the seven deadly sins [245];

e) Do what is more pleasing to God in amusements which are good or indifferent in themselves, or in perfections of supererogation [357], which are shown by obedience, council, general norms of perfection, or divine inspiration;

f) To dispose one’s life, when the actual state or manner of living, ecclesial office, or economic situation [1, 16, 171], has not been chosen in a sincerely or rightly ordered way [174], and change is possible, noteworthy fruits which are very pleasing to God shall come forth for he who desires make his election anew [174].

g) To reform one’s life and state, when the election was rightly made [175], or change is not possible, or when the will is not ready to make an election about matters subject to a changeable election [189]; to embrace: house and family, way of directing and governing its members, the use of their resources for themselves, the poor, and for pious works [189].

a) To form the conscience with instructions or memory of what constitutes mortal and venial sins, deliberate faults, culpable disorder, and pure absence of greater perfection; the general examination with its subjects can be of use [33-42];

c) To examine oneself in the first record of my sins [56], in the daily general examination [43] and for the general confession [44];

d) To reflect over oneself in the contemplations of the life of Christ, after the considerations of persons, words, and deeds, or while eating, looking to eat as Christ ate, in order to imitate the perfections in His manner of conduct [106-108, 114-116, 122-125, 194, 214, 222]; in the examination of the exercise, until a cause is found for the poor outcome of the exercise [77];

e) The particular examination used to remove a particular sin or defect [24-27], acquire the contrary virtue, when an interior vice dominates [245], or to avoid defects and negligence in the spiritual exercises [90];

f) In the first method of prayer, for the constant amendment of life, frequently practiced with regard to the commandments (rules, obligations proper to one’s state), mortal sins, powers of the soul and bodily senses [238-248];

g) To follow the inspirations of the good angel [89, 213, 315], examining well the resolutions and opinions formed in times of fervor, the actual consolation without cause already past [336];

h) To make use of direction from obedience or from the spiritual father [15];

i) To seek and find for oneself the will of God in the election of a state of life [15], or in its reform [189], through the times and way of making an election [175-188], being disposed to enter in these.

121To conquer oneself

The principal end of the Exercises [21]; to keep our bodily nature obedient to reason and all our bodily faculties subject to the higher [87], and reason (the will and intellect together with the memory) obedient to God.

I. Dominion over the senses

Dominion over the senses (interior and exterior) and over the inferior parts (the faculties of the body): are achieved in the Exercises largely through corporeal penance [87], the restraining of the senses [81] and through silence [20, 80]; with promptness upon rising [73, 74] and at the hours of exercise [6], filling the hour completely [12, 13, 19, 128, 254, 255]; doing per diametrum what is contrary to nature, the appetites, or temptation [13, 217, 325]; with interior recollection [74, 78, 130, 206, 229]; recovering an abhorrence for the disorder of one’s actions [63], for the worldly spirit in the use of things (worldly and vain things) [63]; experiencing profound contrition, to the point of tears [4, 55, 87, 89], and divine consolations [316], which call and attract toward heavenly things [316].

II. Dominion of the will for God

Progressive steps:

a) Resolution to avoid all sin, mortal and venial, and all deliberate faults [53, 61, 63, 165, 166, 348-350], and to always choose that which is more conducive to one’s end, the glory of God, or known to be the divine will [23, 151], and in other things, when this is not evident, not to incline oneself one way or the other: toward health, riches, honor, long life, etc., or the opposite [23].

b) To complete the will of God with greater promptness and diligence in all things and every situation [91], resolving to labor with works (poverty, humiliations, sufferings) [97, 98, 147] for love of Christ, who suffered these for me [95, 116], until arriving at the third degree of humility, to embrace actual poverty, and not to flee from humiliation nor suffering, if the greater glory of God is not opposed to this [167, 168, 197].

c) To change one’s affective dispositions, until the point of detesting my sins, the disorder of my works and of the world [63]; to remove from myself every particular disordered affection for a person or thing whether it be good or indifferent in itself [170], in such a way that I do not desire anything or anyone but God alone [1, 16, 150, 154, 237, 338, 342]; and extinguishing actual repugnance toward poverty, humiliation, a short life, etc. [157, 166], or the contrary [157].

d) To order one’s self love, self-will and self-interests, in their roots [189], feeling the pains of the suffering Christ as one’s own [203] and the joy and gladness of the glorious Christ [221], until I see Him as another I; destroying the ownership of what we have and what we are, recognizing with joy that we have received everything from God [233, 234], and that we depend on Him for our very being and works, returning all to God with our desires and liberty [234], trusting solely on the help of His grace, which we ask for in everything, and attributing to Him the glory of all things [237]; finally giving to God all love, loving Him in all things and all things in Him [237, 316].

e) To seek the satisfaction of the heart in God alone [234], having Christ as a consoler [224] and entering into a life of friendship with God, walking in His continual presence [235].

III. Dominion over the understanding and the memory for God

Progressive steps:

a) Dominion over thoughts and the imagination, in the spiritual exercises, with the first and second addition, or their equivalent, upon going to bed, briefly summing up the exercise to be made [73] and upon rising [74], or before entering into the exercise of the hour [131], thinking of where I am going and for what reason [239], and awakening feelings conformed to that which is sought, also presenting to oneself fitting comparisons [74], beginning by placing oneself in the presence of God [75], and then making a composition of place [47]; and throughout the day with the sixth addition [78], having determined materials and particular feelings with which to occupy the thoughts and affect, those very diligently noted in the text for each week [78, 13, 206, 229].

b) To yield understanding of matters of the faith to the authority of the Church [365], and to lay one’s judgment down before Her precepts [353], never seeking offensive reasoning, but defending Her [361].

c) To make a total self-gift of the understanding and memory to God [234], in order to employ them in that alone which is of His greater service, and especially in God Himself, considering Him present in all things and in myself [235], and that in all things He works for me [236]; the perfect through constant contemplation and enlightenment of their understanding, more readily consider, meditate, and contemplate God our Lord as being present in every creature by His essence, presence, and power; and thus when they swear by a creature, they are more able and better disposed than the imperfect to render respect and reverence to their Creator and Lord [39].

d) To correct the practical judgment in what can be chosen or avoided, not only in cases of divine or human precepts, grave or mild [165, 166], but also in regards to what is most in conformity to the divine will [151], keeping watch not only to what is mortal or venial sin, but also to the mere disorder in intention, affection and works [46, 63, 184, 338], always keeping the eye of the intention simple, focusing only on the purpose for which I am created [169], and in every decision considering only reasons of divine service and the good of my soul [181, 182].

e) To reform the formed concepts regarding the value and usefulness of persons and things, and of oneself: knowing the ugliness and malice of each mortal sin committed [57], the lack of conformity between right reason and the disorder in my works, what is irrational and detrimental of the worldly spirit of ostentation, diversion and comfort, in order to establish the corresponding abhorrence, which is the guarantee of amendment [63]; penetrating the mystery of the cross, how much it is valued, desired and experienced for one’s own perfection, peace and interior joy [116, 124] and divine glory [303], what I ought to do and suffer for Christ [197]; with the aim to thus correct the natural judgment which looks at one’s own excellence and happiness as opposed to poverty, humiliation, and suffering [116, 124, 139, 142, 146, 164], in such a way that knowledge of the true life enclosed in the cross, which Christ sets forth, [139] moves me to beg repeatedly in colloquies the grace of actual suffering [147, 156, 168, 199]; to know interiorly what I have received from God in as far as I am and what I have [233, 234], and how I depend on Him for my very being and my works [235]; my littleness in comparison to all men, angels and God [58]; my own frailty in regards to my body [47, 58]; and its evil in regards to the soul, a sore and abscess from which have issued such great sins and iniquities [58], and capable of greater abominations because of original sin [47, 51]; how I count for little in time of desolation, without intense grace and consolation [324]; that it is not in my power to bring about or to have consolations [322], and that I am in need of grace for everything, even to remind me how many times I have fallen into the particular sin which I would like to correct and amend [25]; trying to reach an interior knowledge of my sins, mortal and venial, and of the concrete disorders in my works, in order to correct and amend them [63].

f) To acquire intimate knowledge of Christ, God and Man: of the Eternal Word incarnate [109, 130], of the Lord who has made himself man for me [104], to die for my sins [53, 197], and to go before me in the battle against carnal, sensual, and worldly love [95], so that I may love Him more and with a greater effort, follow Him [104, 130]; of the labors and sufferings of His humanity throughout all His life [116, 195, 196, 206], and of the part that His divinity took in His passion [196], and resurrection [219, 223], in order to more easily form a higher concept of the infinite divine perfections [59, 237], which contra pose the limitations creatures have by participation [237], they extort all love from the heart [316], and detach it from worldly nobility and from the love and pleasure of created things [47, 58, 152].

122The will

I. Human

1. Its dominion for God: total self-gift to perfectly complete the divine will [234]; change affective dispositions to detest what is evil and disordered [63], extinguishing all actual repugnance [157] and ordering all particular love [1, 16, 184, 338], and self-love [189].

2. Its realization:

a) In the exercises: in all of the following spiritual exercises, when we use acts of the will, speaking vocally or mentally with God or with the saints, greater reverence is needed on our part than when we use the understanding [3]; these acts are: to ask for grace in the preparatory prayer, the last preamble and the colloquies, the examinations, methods of prayer and of making an election; to repent [77, 172], grieve [27, 82], blame oneself [54], accuse oneself of faults [243], to pray for forgiveness and pardon from them [43, 241], to propose amendment with the help of grace [43, 61], to give thanks [43, 61, 71], to experience sorrow or joy over the subject [199], to communicate one’s concerns and ask counsel [54]; to make affective acts [3], move the affections [50, 52], to be put to shame and confusion [50], exclamations of wonder with greater affection [60]; to ponder with deep affection how much God has done for me [234]; to give God all my things and myself with them, as one making and offering with deep affection [234].

b) In the interior movements: it is proper of the Creator to enter, leave, make movements in the soul, drawing the whole person into love of God [330]; some interior movement is caused within the soul through which it comes to be inflamed with love for its Creator, and no other created thing can be loved in itself, but only in the Creator of them all [316]; the Lord, properly ordering one’s desires changes their first inclination [16]; to give consolation without cause, without any previous perception or understanding of some object, by means of which such a consolation might come through acts of the understanding or will [330]; in the first time of election God moves and attracts the will, so that without doubting nor being able to doubt, the soul carries out what was proposed [175]; in the experience of consolations and desolations with a preceding cause, the good angel also in part moves the will [176]; one desires only to keep or reject something solely according to what God our Lord will move one’s will to choose [155].

c) God moves secretly in the third time to make an election: beg God to be pleased to move my will and place into my soul what I ought to do regarding the proposed affair, discerning well with my intellect and choosing in conformity with His will [180].

II. Divine

1. Norm of order: always coinciding with that which better leads toward the end for which we are created; we have to accept the events which God disposes; not my will, but Yours be done [290]; once His will is known, we have to put it into practice.

2. To accomplish it:

a) Offering and gift of oneself and all one’s things in order that God be served [5] and dispose all to His will [234].

b) Sincerity in following it: many choose first to marry, and second to serve God in the marriage; in such a manner that they do not go directly to God but desire God to come directly to their disordered affections [169]; the second class of men keep the acquired good in such a way that God comes where he desires [154].

c) To be attentive and diligent to complete the divine will [91]; disposed to it, resolving to labor for love of Christ [98]

3. To know it: in order to complete the divine will it is necessary to know it for oneself or by means of another; many times it is established generally, because always and for everyone the norm of order desired by God is the same; then, in order to know it, it suffices to form and refine one’s conscience and examine oneself; in other cases a general norm does not exist, because what is better conformed to divine service varies according to person and circumstance; the particular arrangements or rules, obedience, spiritual direction [15], inspirations and internal lights [89, 213, 315], examined well [336] can guide one to knowledge of what is more pleasing to God in each case.

III. To seek the will of God for oneself

1. When: it is licit and meritorious to advise another who is capable to follow the evangelical councils, in professing vows [14], and in religion [15], leaving the common state of life of the commandments, marriage and possession of riches [135, 150, 154, 169, 171]; in making the exercises, it is much better, seeking the will of God, that the Creator communicates Himself to the soul, disclosing to him the way in which he could better serve Him in the future [15]; the director ought to be indifferent and leave God to work immediately in the soul [15]; in the exercises, when there is no possibility of a change, or else no ready will to make an election about matters subject to a changeable election, it is very profitable to present a procedure and method for making a reform of one’s life and state [189], in that which regards one’s own person and state [344].

2. With what dispositions: after removing from oneself all disordered affections [1], all affect or repugnance against actual poverty [157], all affection or particular disordered love of things or persons, that they come across in the election or reform [16, 184, 338, 342], in order that the Creator may with greater certainty work in the creature [16].

3. How: the will of God is found:

a) Directly, when God Himself immediately moves and draws the will in such a way that without doubt, nor being able to doubt, the soul carries out what was proposed (1st time) [175], or when through His angels in times of consolation with a preceding cause, or in desolation, God moves and draws the will with persistence in one way or another, or when the spirits induce it toward one direction or another, and from all these by means of the experience of consolation and desolation, and of discernment of various spirits, he can know God’s will with sufficient clarity (2nd time) [176].

b) Indirectly, when we deduce what the will of God is for us, reasoning freely and tranquilly with our natural potencies (3rd time), what appears to be in greater accordance with divine service (1st method) [155, 182], or what we feel inclined toward by means of ordered affection (2nd method) [184, 338]; after having diligently offered this election to God in prayer and having begged Him to receive and confirm it, if it is for His greater service and praise [183, 188].

4. Where:

a) The first and second times have a place in the hours of exercises themselves, contemplating the mysteries of the life of Christ [135], inquiring at the beginning in which state or way of life does the Divine Majesty wish us to serve Him [135], and that He places this in our will with His movements [155].

b) When God does not communicate Himself directly, or communicates Himself without sufficient clarity, one should present to themselves the methods of the 3rd time, dedicating a special time to these by way of exercise; in the 1st method, asking God at the beginning, that with the grace He desires to place in my soul, by the faithful discernment of the understanding, it may be strengthened with divine illumination [2], of that which may be for His greater glory and praise, and move my will to choose in conformity to His most holy will [180]; already having considered the pros and cons of one side or the other, attending only to the divine service, to see where reason more inclines one to [181, 182]; which requires one to seek real indifference, in such a way that it is not more inclined, nor attached toward taking a thing than to leaving it, nor more toward leaving it than taking it [179]; in the 2nd method, an actual affection is assumed and ordered; and if from this point it becomes fully evident [342], one can follow their impulse as coming from the divine will, since the love of God which inspires the act descends from above [184, 338]; in order to assure oneself, one should examine the motive of their affection towards a thing, if it is for God alone [184], or for a person, if it is for God, being attentive that God may shine forth in the reason for which I have greater love [338]; one should see how they would counsel another person in their situation, someone for whom they desire all perfection [185, 399], and mentally place oneself at the point of death [186, 340] and final judgment [187, 341],to conceptualize what one would think of the present choice.

c) In less important decisions, such as the amount of penance [89], or food [213], to know the will of God in the proper medium, one begins with much penance and abstinence, watching that one does not fall into notable sickness [98, 213]; if the consolation that is sought with penance delays in coming, make an alteration, having two or three days of penance and two or three days without [89]; and through changes of this sort God often enables each to know what is right for themselves [89]; in greater abstinence, many times God communicates interior lights, consolations and divine inspirations, which guide one to the mean suitable to oneself [213]; and without this, if the person experiences in such abstinence a lack of physical energy and disposition to carry on the present spiritual exercises, one will soon be able to judge what is more suitable to one’s own bodily sustenance [213]; thus we will have made an application of the direct and indirect methods of knowing the will of God.

Chapter 3: Guide for the Reading of the Book of the Exercises

123It is our intention to clarify some points that can present difficulty in order to facilitate the reading and comprehension of the Ignatian text. We will use the notes of Fathers Calveras, M. Iglesias, Ubillos, Codina, Oraá, Guillermo Furlong, J. L. Torres Pardo, I. Iparaguirre, I. Casanovas, J. Grasset, etc. We ought not to forget that we are before a text written in old Spanish with a bit of a Baroque style.

124Certainly the Exercises are “made”, not studied, but for those who have to “give” them, in addition to personal experience of having “made” or “taken” them, one also has to study them in order to be able to “give them” with greater profit.

125The numbers between brackets [ ] refer to the book of the Spiritual Exercises94 (which strictly speaking is a “Notebook of points”), according to the division made by Father Codina.

126[1] The “Annotations” are a preparation or introduction to the Exercises. They are thus divided:

[1] Nature and end of the exercises.

[2-3] General method of procedure.

[4] Parts and length.

[5] Fundamental disposition of the exercitant.

[6-17] Conduct of the director in respect to the exercitant.

[18-20] Adaptations for the exercitants.

[1] “Annotations”: from the title placed by the saint to the “annotations”, one can deduce that he did not write this book simply to be read, nor for whoever would use it for their studies and meditation. The title itself indicates to us that he who makes the Exercises, ought to receive them, understanding above all that having experienced them for himself, he is found well versed in this sacred art. “Disordered affections” [evil and dangerous loves]: is the love, by excess or defect that we have toward a person or thing. Toward persons: parents, friends, oneself; toward things: money, pleasures, honor, fame, bodily or spiritual goods in general.

They are not only evil, those disordered affections which are sins, but also those affections that one has toward things not for their spiritual and moral value exacted from the will of God, but against Him, or disregarding Him, or not giving the esteem and value which corresponds to them (Cf. 1 Corinthians 7:29-32). Not only what is sinful is evil, but also not to obey purely and uprightly the reasons of divine service and love in regards to that which is of itself indifferent and good: “other spiritual operations”: reform of life, election of a state, etc.

[2] “History”: the theme or topic of the mystery or truth of faith that one meditates or contemplates upon. “Enlightened”: illumined. “Not in knowing much… but the feeling and taste of interior things”: this last phrase is a synthesis of the entire transcendental method and fundamental principle in directing the exercitant.

[4] “Subject matter”: that which is principally sought in the meditations of each week.

[5] “With great spirit and liberality”: The disposition of the soul, the saint recommended, should be exposed, seeking to convince and persuade all those who come to make the Exercises, either in private or in common. This liberality which has to be instilled, the offering of oneself entirely to the Divine Majesty, in order to complete entirely the will of their Creator and Lord, consists in two things, namely: that one desires to be abundantly enlightened in their understanding. “What shall I do, Lord?” (Cf. Heb. 22:10); and that they desire to complete with their will that which will lead them to recognize: Lord, “teach me to do your will” (Cf. Ps. 143:10). This double prayer is very necessary.

[13] “To conquer”: to defeat. “To accustom himself”: to habituate oneself.

[14, 15] “Personal qualities”: capacity.

[15] “Still”: nonetheless.

[16] “To be attached”: affected, disposed toward. “Inordinately”: because one does not seek solely that the soul is not inclined toward something less ordered, but that one is not inordinately inclined toward anything, whether it be a lesser good, or something good and ideal. Since even toward our own goods we can become inordinately affected, it may be that we desire some good not for a good end, or despite the thing being in itself good, it is nonetheless not a fitting means to the end; or also, without reflection, precipitously, or with too much ardor or anxiety, we feel drawn toward it. All this extends to the word inordinately. “Benefice”: ecclesial office with attached revenues.

[18, 19, 20] These three last annotations are of great importance. In these are given the basic principles of the method by which one must adapt the exercises when they cannot be given in their most complete and pure form- isolated and for a month- for the lack of disposition, capacity or time on the half of the exercitant. Here one can see a variety of forms for the exercises, as foreseen by St. Ignatius: light, open, mild. Here he indicates the subject matter, end and proper methods of each of these forms.

[18] “Uneducated”: without strong constitution. “Of little intelligence”: can be interpreted diversely: lacking in disposition or aptitude, weak constitution, immature, etc.

[20] “In the order in which they follow”: the Vulgate adds here: “and it is convenient to write a summary of the things, so that they do not escape the memory.” “Ordinarily” can also mean “by an appropriate means”.

127[21] “Some disordered affection”: In the exposition of the goal of the exercises, a triple direction is noted. Some prefer to see in the exercises a framework to prepare and dispose the soul that, rightly ordered, may be able to love and serve His Divine Majesty in everything (Casanovas, Calveras). Others consider them more as a school of prayer, a means of intimate union with God (Peeters). Ultimately, a third group believes that the exercises are centered on the election (Hummelauer, Iglesias, Grandmaison). “Presupposition”: that which one proposes the initial postulation. The basis of success is that an atmosphere of confidence, mutual understanding, be established between the director and the one directed from the beginning.

128[22] “The proposition”: that which a neighbor proposes or says. “…seek all the suitable means to bring him to mean it (the proposition) well, and save himself”: accepting the true doctrine in that point, he frees himself from error in the faith, and places himself on the road of salvation (Calveras). Others understand this to mean: “to save the proposition of one’s neighbor”.

129[23] “Principle and foundation”: These words, in the mind of the saint, are not synonymous, for principle refers to the theory and foundation to the practice. The whole structure and building of the Spiritual Exercises rests on this meditation. “Free ourselves from them”: to uproot those loves which bring us toward what is evil and dangerous… until we detest them… to the point that we strip ourselves of the love even for good and innocent things, when we seek them for human motives and not for the love of God, or perhaps, ordering the naturally honest ones, exchanging the natural affection we have toward things for a supernatural affection. “It is necessary to make ourselves indifferent”: that is, in which way we ought to conduct ourselves with created things, by means of our own conquest, as if we feel no inclination or repugnance toward them, denying our senses, our likes and dislikes. This is the necessary endeavor by which we strive to achieve such a degree of perfection, exalted beyond doubt, in such a way that we use or refrain from creatures “only inasmuchas”, neither more or less than what our final end requires. The Ignatian indifference is not of the senses [excluding all contrary sensible affection], but of the will; it is not stupidity, it is rational; it is not impotence but a free and mastering will capable of dedicating oneself to things without letting oneself to be dominated by them; it is not inhumane, but is the submission of the appetite to reason, and reason to God; it is not stoicism: it is Christian because one gives everything to God; it is not apathy but enthusiasm like that of the saints and martyrs; it doesn’t desire to kill our initiatives, but to channel them, incite them, inflame them. Only before sin can there be no indifference but a positive aversion. “We want not”: in so far as we seek it. It’s more about affection.

130[24] “Three times, and two to examine oneself”: the regulation of the particular examination is always considered as one of the most characteristic and original pieces of St. Ignatius. In concise form, concrete and practical, it has been known to synthesize this movement of control and analysis which is so necessary to the whole process, its subject and likewise its spirit and has always been used in the Church, above all among the Fathers of the desert. Even pagan philosophers like Pythagoreans and Stoics recommend it. It is a practice which has its function within its scheme, and the individual must employ it in conformity to his needs and way of being. Having considered these norms isolated from the whole, and having forgotten that St. Ignatius gives them to the director, so that he applies them in keeping with his prudence and the necessity of the one directed, they (pagan philosophers) have judged them absurdly as pernicious spiritual accountability or an egocentric re-concentration of one’s whole being.

[25] “after eating”: makes reference to the midday meal of lunch, since in these times it was common not to have breakfast. “what one wants”: that which one desires. “Then”: consequently. “To amend”: to correct. “g” or “G”: It was customary to put the initial letter of the word corresponding to the sin which one aspires to eradicate, or the virtue which one desires to advance in. It was commonly advised for beginners to start by fighting against gluttony [G].

[33] “immediately”: at once.

[35] “delay”: brief delay.

[37] “the two persons”: one who sins and the one whom the sin hurts or wrongs.

133[46] “all my intentions, actions and operations”: During the time of prayer often many intentions [thoughts, desires], actions and operations [of the mind and body] come to us, we must ask in the preparatory prayer that all interior and exterior activity be directed to God.

This preparatory prayer is always the same for every meditation; not only in the prayer but always and in every moment we must repeat it, so as to order all our actions to the greater glory of God. This is the only piece which is repeated in all the exercises, because the principle and foundation is the norm of order for each and every one of life’s actions.

It is proper of the rational creature to help himself, cooperating freely with divine grace. Even with the rebellious angels, nothing was lacking to them on the part of the most gracious and liberal Creator, but they were lacking of themselves. Likewise, all who sin, who perish, do so by their own fault, not wanting to help themselves. “Then”: consequently.

138[73] The “additions” or annotations, are notes of a secondary character aiming to assist the exercitant in the most advantageous manner, achieving the end with greater security. They also serve to orient the powers of the soul and regulate the senses, the imagination, and the body itself, not only during the time of the meditations, but for the rest of the day. For even if, perhaps, they are already forgiven by mercy – I say perhaps because we certainly are unable to do this – nevertheless, we must here consider what we have done through our own fault, and not what, by the grace of God, our state happens to be now. Since this is a gift of God’s mercy, which is entirely ours; and what is proposed for us to meditate upon in this exercise is what is ours and what has come forth from us. This meditation is very valuable even for those who in their entire lives have never been conscious of any sin other than venial, because it reveals that a single venial sin deliberately committed is such that God most justly withdraws from the soul; and the soul abandoned to itself, to where would it not be cast down? Further, in all justice, how will one who remembers having committed mortal sins feel? If once we separate ourselves from the right path, to where would we not have strayed, Lord, if your right hand had not confined us to your path? [cf. Ps.85:12].

It is worthwhile to illustrate these three degrees of humility with an example: Someone has suffered a great loss in his interests or of his honor.

The first manner of humility: one would not in any way lay claim to his rights, if this could only be done by committing mortal sin.

The second manner of humility: neither would one want to commit a venial sin in order to pursue his own rights, if they couldn’t be claimed without incurring any class of sin.

The third manner of humility: one will take the loss as gain in Christ, infamy as honor; and he will lay no claims but will take it in silence and with joy in the Lord, in as far as the glory of God is equal. This is, in so far as neither the accomplishment of duty nor any other obligation is breached, because if not, there would be no equal glory of God, and therefore would be legitimately defended, and this would not violate the proposition of the third manner of humility, conserving these holy sentiments in his heart, and having the soul disposed in such a way that if by chance the just defense is without effect, as it is not rare to happen, not only does he bear it with patience but he rejoices in the double honor which he had been worthy of in Christ and with Christ. “Worthless”: meaning a “fool”, in the sense of the word in the times of St. Ignatius.
