151[230] In this contemplation, St. Ignatius bridges the atmosphere of the retreat with the real-life situation of exercitant magnificently. In a surpassing and transcendent way, he condenses the most vital elements of the exercises, enabling one to see the trivialities of life, service, and the possibility to transform these in pure love of God. In this way, life can be a continuous exercise of love, because it will be a continual service. It will also be the most fitting response to the friendship offered by God. By means of this interchange of love made by the mutual self-offering, he enters into formal friendship with God, which later he will live out in daily life.

[234] This colloquy, synthesis of the total self-offering that St. Ignatius desires in the exercises and expression of the exchange of friendship begun with God, has been popularized in the form of prayer.

[234-237] The following four points are accustomed to produce a bit of confusion in some, because the distinction between them is not sufficiently clear, seeing that the first point contains within it the second and third.

To suggest some remedy to this inconvenience, they ought to be distinguished by their forms. In keeping with the text of St. Ignatius, we contemplate in the first point the benefits in general that God has or has not bestowed upon us, that is, with a firm hope we trust that from His love has come, comes to us now, and will always come the greatest goods.

In the second point, we contemplate that God grants us those benefits, because He is present in all those things in which He communicates His goods, and in ourselves: in such a way that He personally does us good in all things. For this reason He certainly adds much love to the benefits.

In the third point we contemplate God, who creates these benefits for us, not only being present to us and to all other creatures for our sake, but also laboring, and in a certain sense working in us and in the rest of creation, helping us and all creatures in order to do good to us. If such a trait is found in any benefactor it greatly increases love’s significance, but, in God, it comes from an entirely inexplicable and infinite love; in God, although He bestows true acts to secondary causes, nevertheless, He himself, through his concurrence, also works in them for our good.

“Liberty”: not an arbitrary freedom, but that liberty by which we are masters of ourselves, without any external impediment to part us. “That I have and possess”: “have” refers to what we have of ourselves, interior and personal goods of the soul and body. “Possess” refers more to external goods. “All is Thine”: a second title: You have given it to me, and because of this I freely return it to You, for the end that You may dispose of it according to all Your will.

Hereafter, the saint teaches us with discretion what this change ought to consist of, namely:

1. Insisting more on prayer and meditation.

2. That we examine ourselves a lot, our conscience, our actions, and all of our things.

3. We do something more and exercise penance with greater abundance, in a manner adapted or fitting to us, to our state and our composition. Desolation stupefies us in this triple exercise of examination and penance. Later, contrary, contrariis curanda. We hope that when desolation pursues us we shall have put into practice what St. Ignatius says, since it is so very advantageous in such a state!

Likewise, one who establishes himself in another’s house would be at risk of eviction when the owner appeared. It is notable that the Saint does not say: sin of pride, nor simply pride, but perfunctorily some pride, in order that we understand that the slightest amount of pride or the least bit of self-complacency greatly displeases God, who not infrequently deprives us of His heavenly consolations on account of these small acts of vain complacency. We must avoid particularly in consolation to become vain or vainly believe ourselves to be secure. We ought to trust solely in the mercy of God, and accredit to Him alone the goods that we have received.

Since he is the enemy, he does not expect to bring the soul to evil easily, but he still tempts so as to block its advantage, or at least to lower and afflict it; and in conformity with his hatred, it pleases him at first to vex the soul, not without hope of impeding some greater good in this manner and eventually dragging the soul to evil.

Think for example of how many souls the devil has lost or certainly impeded, or loses or impedes every day, by means of his deceits, indiscrete zeal, and many disordered devotions; nonetheless, his astuteness will be easily eluded by the truly humble and, above all, the obedient soul. Chapter 6: Retreat day for laity

168As a last chapter of the supplements of this directory, we shall indicate some elements in regard to the application of the Exercises.

Often Catholic schools ask for accompaniment in a day of retreat for a particular grade. Generally these are not the best conditions to be able to work with secure fruit. Often it happens that prejudices arise in regard to the youth, against the formation that we would like them to receive and that, in most cases, they do not receive. But this challenge makes pastoral work even more exhilarating. Finally, Christ “died for all” (2 Cor. 5:15) and “I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some” (1 Cor. 9:22), as St. Paul has exemplified.

169If you think about doing a retreat day for the whole school, always treating them according to divisions, it would be fitting to start by the upper grades and then follow with the younger ones. Normally it shouldn’t be done in silence, not only because they are not accustomed to this, but moreover, because in the few free hours very little would be able to be accomplished.

Experience tells us that accompanying the youth in these retreat days (encounters, festivals, gatherings, conferences, get-togethers…or whatever you want to call them) and, although in fact it may not even be an entire day, but only a few hours, the fruits that are obtained are many and qualified, given that they follow a determined schedule and do not waste time in demagogy and pastoral populism which are a failure and a pitiful waste of time.

170We also point out some things that ought to be carefully prepared:

The choice of place where the activities will unfold:

- Space for all to meet.

- Places for discussion groups.

- Dining hall.

- Chapel for the praying of the Rosary, confessions, and the Holy Mass.

The general management of the day (materials for writing: paper, pens, etc.);

- Liturgist, lectors, handout with the Mass responses and songs, choir, rosaries and how to pray it, etc.;

- Leaders for the group discussions.

Schedule

171The schedule, improved on several occasions, is more or less the following:

1.

9:30AM-10:15AM:

a. Make an introduction here, explaining what we desire to do in these hours, without being afraid to take time for the captatio, to capture the attention of the youth …

b. Develop the 1st topic for reflection: The Blessed Virgin, Who is she? How she loves us, helps and protects us, how we ought to love her, the devotion we should have, concrete examples, the Rosary, pilgrimages, the Patroness of our country…

10:15AM-10:45AM:

c. Form discussion groups of approximately 6 students per grade with one chosen leader from among themselves (better to know beforehand who they shall be) and provide a list with roughly 6 substantial questions regarding the given topic so they can later discuss it for about 30 minutes, the leader writing on a paper the responses of the youth. (This method was formerly called the Phillips 66).

… Break.

2.

11:15AM-12PM:

2nd topic for reflection: The life of purity. What is it? It is possible. It is beautiful. It is safe. Negative experiences. The great challenge in a pansexual civilization, where all is reduced to sex. Heroic examples. (6th and 9th Commandments).

12 -12:30PM: Discussion groups.

…Break.

1PM: Lunch and Recreation.

3.

2-2:45PM:

3rd topic for reflection: Family life. The relationship between parents, siblings, and other family members. What are we able to do and what do we have to do? Actual difficulties and how to overcome them. “Training” in order to build a family later. (4th Commandment)

2:45PM.-3:15PM: Group discussions.

4.

3:15PM-3:45PM:

A plenary talk with all the groups, pooling together what was said by the youth in their discussions.

…Break.

5.

4PM.

4th topic for reflection: The mercy of God, how to confess and why, the greatness of God’s forgiveness, mutual help for oneself… Normally this should be in the Chapel. Instead of a discussion, pray the Rosary. Confessions. It is a time of silence.

6.

4:45PM Holy Mass: Homily on the Sunday Mass and Eucharistic devotion.

5:30PM Snack. End of the day.

172Follow-up

Take advantage of the enthusiasm that the youth will have in order to boost the Eucharistic and Penitential liturgies in school.

The same follows for all other pastoral initiatives to be realized at the school. Think especially of a way to help those who would like to attend universities.

See for the future experience, who has the subiectum, and could be invited to the 5 day Spiritual Exercises.
